He is a Chinese Australian character, and what I like about this novel is that you've got a journey, you've got a family history story that is doing something fresh, taking us into Australian history and doing it through this figure of the jiāngshī, the Chinese hopping vampire. It's clever and playful at the same time.

SL: I have trouble with books where one of the characters is a ghost or a zombie because I get distracted by thinking about the logistics.

I was more drawn to the historical elements of the family story that build up this picture of how this family has evolved over four generations, and how the family's Chinese heritage has been whitewashed. That's what really appealed to me.

I wanted to spend more time with the first two characters we meet, Pan Bo Lin and his to-be wife, Bridget. They were fascinating. I rushed through the zombie bits because I wanted to get back to the family.

CN: I was also really moved by the stories from the past. I loved meeting the multiple generations of this family; I think Steve MinOn does it so well.

The juxtaposition of that with this zombie who keeps losing bits of his body and attacking people and sucking the life out of them as he moves further north towards Innisfail — it's really exciting and unusual. I'm always thrilled when Aussie authors just go for it with a really bonkers idea. I found this a very pleasurable read.

My Heart at Evening by Konrad Muller

Henry Hellyer, a 19th-century English surveyor and architect, "was a complex historical figure", Muller told The Book Show. (Supplied: Evercreech Editions)

DF: My Heart at Evening is set in 1832 in Van Diemen's Land. A man is sent to learn what's happened to Henry Hellyer, a real-life figure. We know how Hellyer died — the question is why did he die? Why did he kill himself? Various people come and reveal their interpretations of what happened in this kind of Rashomon-style set-up.

One possibility is he committed suicide because he was gay, and the shame of being homosexual at that time makes it completely plausible. Or perhaps it was because of the violence and the brutalisation of colonisation. It could be all of these things or none of them — that's the heart of mystery and darkness in this very Joseph Conradian novel.

KE: I loved the voice of this novel. From the very first page, I thought this is doing something so assured — the narrator is ostensibly addressing his beloved. It's almost a second-person telling of a story that she will never receive — it's like a letter that is never sent.

And then there's all of that rich colonial context which, as Sarah said, almost feels Dickensian. There's a real 19th-century style to it and then overlaying it there's all this really interesting convict history. There's the Van Diemen's Land Company, which really existed and played a role similar to the East India Company, so it's not that you've got a government who's shaping this terrible, violent colonial moment; you've got corporate entities committing violence against the land and Aboriginal people.

Some of it's almost happening at the edge of the main character's eyesight. He can't even quite look at it. It's so beautifully done.

CN: I love that this is essentially a detective novel. We've got a mystery to solve; we're going to interview various people and figure out what happened.

And I love that it's such an Australian novel in that our detective is a convict, and it's a story that could only be set in this place. I think that's really delicious.

SL: It's not just a detective novel; it draws on that classic trope of Agatha Christie of the locked-room mystery as well. It's like a red herring, but it's a delightful element within the story, which gives levity to the brooding elements in the book.

KE: And the rogues and the ratbags and the convict cant [street slang] that he plays around with as well.

CN: I love that everyone who gets interviewed are such specific characters. There is a series of blokes, and they could all blur into one, but they're so clear, whether it be a flourish of a scarf or the way they speak. I think it's very carefully done.

DF: It's incredibly impressive for a debut novelist to have such well-rounded characterisation.

SL: I also found it interesting each of those interviews raised more questions than they answered. The picture gets more complicated. Even at the end, there was another revelation. Muller keeps layering different perspectives, one on top of each other.

Fierceland by Omar Musa

Musa won the 2026 Victorian Premier's Prize for Fiction for Fierceland. (Supplied: Penguin)

SL: This is a book about complicity and history that draws on Omar Musa's own connections to his family in Borneo.

It's about a palm oil baron, Yusuf, and his children. One is an artist, Rozana, who's a bit of a rebel who hasn't found her place. Her brother Harun lives in LA. He's developing some interesting technology using virtual reality to recreate forests that in the real world have been destroyed by the palm oil industry.

This is a story of these two characters grappling with their father's legacy. The timeline moves around — we go back with them as children to visit the plantations, to visit the forest before it's destroyed, and then we're with them as they're reckoning with their father's death.

KE: And importantly, the forest itself is one of the voices in the novel.

SL: And so are the people who are working on the plantation. He's giving voice to people and things that don't often have a voice.

KE: There are so many different voices and perspectives in this novel. It's so rich and one of the things that I like about it is how judicious he is about the use of things like the voice of the forest because too much of that would have been hard going. Because Musa is a musician and a rapper and a performer and a visual artist, I feel as though the narrative rhythms of this book are a really important part of it.

I also liked the way that it took us into the region and placed us in it — I didn't know enough about Malaysian Borneo.

CN: It's the second novel in a row where we're grappling with Joseph Conrad; we were doing that with Konrad Muller but obviously this book has very direct references to Conrad, who wrote a lot about Borneo, but also, we've got the ill-fated troop up the river. It's interesting that we're getting a Heart of Darkness theme emerging on the list.

DF: And as in Muller, early on, we're told there's a traumatic event. We know what it is, but there are still questions around it. There are a few interpretations given by the people around Yusuf, but it's never concretely said exactly what happened.

I really loved the way it shows familial camaraderie in what is a dysfunctional family where you have two children who are so rich they never really need to work again. I did find Rozana's adult voice a bit odd — she's 32, but she speaks like someone much younger. I don't think that was convincingly explained. In any case, I thought that Yusuf and the people around Yusuf, these side characters and their voices, were more interesting.

I would love to see the working drafts of this novel's development because there's so much history, there's so much voice. There is a real richness in Musa's language, especially in those more experimental sections when he takes the brakes off.

This could have been a really great work of creative non-fiction with all of its history, its languages, its different voices, including the forest.

But I feel like some of the impulses animating his experimentation are constrained by the more conventional chapters. I don't think the sections quite cohere.

SL: I really wanted to love this book because of all of those elements, and there's some just truly exquisite writing, but, like Declan, the pieces didn't quite come together for me.

I found moving around in the timeline, also moving with perspective, it didn't build into a complete whole. This trend of using alternating chapters and voices — I just want Australian writers to go deep and give me the whole story without feeling the need to show that this is one person's perspective and this is another's. Just give me the total book.

CN: I was thinking about the same thing, Sarah. With so many of these novels, there's one strand of the story I like better than the other, and sometimes I'm reading one chapter faster because I want to get back to the bit I like. That's a danger with this type of writing, right? It's the case for quite a few books on this list, that they're a little lopsided in the reading.

Little World by Josephine Rowe

Rowe's debut novel, A Loving, Faithful Animal, was longlisted for the 2017 Miles Franklin Literary Award. (Supplied: Black Inc.)

DF: This book is about a saint, but she's an unusual saint in that the Vatican don't seem to be aware of her. It's a girl who has a body that does not decompose, and the story is about the ways in which her incorruptible saintly body and existence impact the lives of the people she comes into contact with, which include a retired engineer living near Broome in the 1950s and three women in the 70s who are travelling across Australia in a van, a lesbian couple and a woman who's a bit older called Mathilde.

The language is stunning. Josephine Rowe writes like an angel. The novel is very elliptical; how willing the reader is to sit with its suggestive aspects will determine how much they get out of it.

For me, the biggest impact the novel has is how very compactly, very succinctly, very beautifully Josephine Rowe reflects upon the lives of women. It's this communion between Mathilde and the saint, where they're women who are struggling with violence, both geopolitical and personal, and how they find some kind of solace in one another.

KE: I like the fact that it's such an odd take on an Australian history. I thought it was so fresh and surprising and odd and restrained, in a good way.

It worked as a really short novel. If it had been a sprawling 400-page novel doing this, taking all these perspectives, I think I would've needed to lie down. But having it compressed and poetic like this worked for me.

CN: It works for me too. Anyone who can put that much into 130 pages is just so clever. I think it's a pretty perfect little object.

You Must Remember This by Sean Wilson

You Must Remember This started out as a play inspired by Wilson's observations of his grandmother's experience of dementia. (Supplied: Simon & Schuster)

CN: We're with a character called Grace. She is an elderly woman and at the start of the book, we're remembering things with her when, all of a sudden, we look down with her at her feet and we realise that she is walking along a highway, there are cars whizzing by, it's in the middle of the night and she had no idea how she got there.

We realise this is a character with Alzheimer's disease, and we are with her as time and memory shifts. There are some really clever ways that Sean Wilson does this, including starting the book at chapter 10, and the chapters shift as we move around in time and Grace's memory.

We have scenes in the modern day where her daughter is trying to connect with her and is getting increasingly frustrated. But we also go back to Grace's childhood in Perth, which we learn was incredibly difficult, with an alcoholic, cruel mother.

This is a really short, beautiful book that tells the story of dementia in a really beautiful and important way, because I don't think there's a lot of fiction that tries to take dementia head on and give the characters respect and time to really explore what it might be like to experience it.

SL: I felt like its biggest strength was taking us into the confusing world of a person with dementia but giving that person a history and a present and situating them in a place, not just disregarding them because they no longer make sense to the outside world.

CN: Again, we've got that alternating chapter approach, with Grace in the present day and going back to different parts of her story. Once again, I was more drawn to the stuff in the past than the present day.

The character of her mother, Annie, reminded me of Dolly Pickles from Cloudstreet: this very loud, once beautiful and now cruel alcoholic woman.

She was such a strong character that at times I felt she wanted to become our main character. I wanted more of Annie.

SL: I thought the writing was exquisite. Being at sea is something I don't typically enjoy, but I liked being at sea with Grace and discovering what's going on with her. I felt safe in the author's hands and trusted that he was going to take me somewhere.

I found it a very satisfying read for those reasons. Claire says that Little World was a perfect book — for me, You Must Remember This was a perfect nugget of a book. It didn't overextend itself and while the remembrances of the past were very vibrant and alive, I felt the danger of Grace's present situation very much.

CN: It's another book that doesn't overstay its welcome, much like Little World and My Heart at Evening. I think Australian fiction can get really shaggy and sometimes needs another edit and to see some books that actually tell the story they need to tell and then finish is really lovely.

Snubs, surprises and tips

CN: I would have loved to have seen Toni Jordan make the shortlist for her novel Tenderfoot. I think it's the best novel she's ever written.

I still think this is an excellent list. I don't know what will win but I would enjoy it if First Name Second Name won just for being weird and wonderful.

DF: My snub is Olivia De Zilva's Plastic Budgie, put out by Pink Shorts Press, a great small publisher. It reminded me of [American novelist] Lynne Tillman who I adore. Elegy, Southwest by Madeleine Watts was quite moving and I would have also liked to see that on the shortlist.

Listen to ABC RN's The Bookshelf The latest and best fiction reviewed by a team of dedicated bibliophiles.

The winner I think is going to be Omar Musa. Prize judging tends to be splitting the difference between books people love and books they can agree upon. I don't know what the judges will love, but I think they'll probably agree upon Omar Musa.

I think Konrad Muller should win. It was just such a wow debut.

SL: I would have liked to see Charlotte McConnaghy's Wild Dark Shore on the list — it's nice to see Miles Franklin being a little bit more popular and I really loved that book.

While I'd like You Must Remember This to win, I also think Fierceland will win.

KE: I would love to see My Heart at Evening win, but I can never guess these things. I think it's a really interesting shortlist.

World.title: Fan fault shuts Sydney's M5 in morning rush, causing 10km of traffic chaos
World.content:
Traffic on the M5 motorway has been backed up for more than 10 kilometres due to the closure of city-bound lanes on the M5.

Transurban, which operates the road, closed the tunnel earlier this morning in order to repair a ventilator fan.

Aerial footage and the Live Traffic website show cars backed up from the closure point near Beverly Hills, all the way to Milperra.

Transport for New South Wales coordinator-general Howard Collins urged drivers to avoid the area as the delays are not expected to be resolved until after the morning peak.

"I'd ask people, if you don't need to travel in that area, maybe stay at home or do something different and if you do need to travel, take your time, be patient with people," Mr Collins said.

He said diversions were in place via King Georges Road and Stoney Creek Road, and the M8 is open, but those roads were also heavily congested.

Mr Collins said Transurban crews were at the site working to repair the fan, work which would require a crane.

"It's the physical nature of this fan, which needs to be removed, does negate anyone using the tunnel," he said.

"The engineers are all down there, they're working as hard as they can … but it's going to take time.

"Obviously this was an undiscovered fault which they found overnight."

'Safe course of action'

General Manager of WestConnex at Transurban, Denise Kelly, told 702 ABC Sydney it was deemed unsafe to wait until this evening to remove the fan.

"That was a question we asked ourselves, and we assessed the safety situation and safety is the priority, and we decided that the safe course of action was to remove it now," Ms Kelly said.

She declined to commit to blanket toll relief to compensate drivers impacted by the incident, but individual drivers can contact the company to seek a refund.

"There are plenty of people paying tolls all around Sydney this morning and so it wouldn't be right for some people to be refunded when they weren't actually inconvenienced," Ms Kelly said.

She said crews were working towards reopening the tunnel before the afternoon peak.

World.title: ‘No-one’s vaping in the gym’: Doueihi apologises for Tigers walkout as he and Marshall address club culture
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘No-one’s vaping in the gym’: Doueihi apologises for Tigers walkout as he and Marshall address club culture Dan Walsh and Adrian Proszenko Updated July 29, 2026 — 10:10am ,first published July 29, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adam Doueihi has apologised to Tigers fans and his teammates after controversially standing himself down from playing as coach Benji Marshall addressed allegations of players using e-cigarettes during training sessions. Doueihi returned to training on Tuesday and addressed teammates, having clashed with Marshall over the coach’s decision to move him from the halves for last week’s game against the Raiders, which the Tigers lost 56-10. Adam Doueihi returned to Wests Tigers training on Tuesday. Audrey Richardson An irate Doueihi took the opportunity to speak his mind, telling the coach he was fed up with the lack of accountability and professionalism that had led to another failed NRL campaign, and told Marshall he would not be playing against Canberra. Doueihi raised several issues over standards at the club, though refused to elaborate on Wednesday morning as he reiterated that he is committed to his three-year deal with the Tigers and is not eyeing an early exit.



“I should’ve played,” Doueihi said, conceding he took Marshall’s positional call “the wrong way”. “It hurt watching the boys on the weekend that I wasn’t out there … I’ve had a really, really good conversation with Benji, Shaun and the club about my care-factor for the club. Adam Doueihi and Benji Marshall at training on Tuesday. Audrey Richardson “I play and wear my heart on my sleeve. I know it’s hard for our fans to see. I let them down on the weekend. “I’m happy to wear all the criticism … Did I want to bring that noise to the club? No, that wasn’t my intention. I had a really good conversation with [my teammates] after.”



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Tigers name Adam Doueihi at halfback for Eels clash Minutes earlier, Marshall denied suggestions of double standards among the playing group, as well as reports that Tigers players have been vaping in the gym, claiming the stories were “fabricated”, but acknowledged players using e-cigarettes is an issue for the club. “There are issues that if they are issues, we’ll definitely address internally among the players,” Marshall said. I can tell you now that no one’s vaped in the gym, that’s actually fabricated or misinformation. “Is there a vaping problem? Probably with players, but like with young men, you can’t tell them whether to vape or smoke or whatnot, and I definitely can’t control what they do 24/7, and I’m not with them all the time, so I don’t feel like there’s a culture problem. “If we’re talking about standards and that, there’s probably a few things we might have walked past recently that we need to address ... whatever the concerns were from Adam’s perspective, they were all dealt with in the room.”



Marshall said his decision to recall Doueihi immediately into his starting side against the Eels, at the expense of rookie Javon Andrews, was the best call in pursuit of a win. “I didn’t feel disrespected [by Doueihi’s withdrawal],” Marshall said. “What I could see was a young guy who needed support and wasn’t in the head space to play … I saw a guy who was hurting and who wasn’t in the position to play. You can’t force that.” The development came just 24 hours after Doueihi held peace talks with Marshall, chief executive Shaun Mielekamp and football manager Pat Richards, with the rugby league news cycle dominated by the latest drama to engulf the joint-venture. More to come.

World.title: Victorian Labor leadership LIVE: Premier Ben Carroll mulls cabinet appointments following Jacinta Allan’s resignation
World.content:
As politicians arrive at Spring Street for another sitting of Victorian Parliament, Labor MPs congratulated Jacinta Allan on her long career in politics after The Age reported last night she would not recontest her seat of Bendigo East.

“I congratulated her on an incredible career and as a great servant of the Labor Party and as a woman who has made an extraordinary contribution to the people of Victoria,” said former health minister Mary-Anne Thomas, an ally of Allan.

Former health minister Mary-Anne Thomas last year. Simon Schluter

“It’s always moving when a dear friend and a person who has served with such distinction, their career comes to an end. But I’m sure that she’s looking forward to some much-needed time with her family.”

Ports Minister Melissa Horne, who had privately advocated for a royal commission, thanked Allan for her service but said the leadership change was “an opportunity to reset”.

World.title: Millions tune in as Qantas jet completes 24-hour non-stop flight
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Millions tune in as Qantas jet completes 24-hour non-stop flight Chris Zappone July 29, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas’ Project Sunrise plane has touched down in Toulouse after flying non-stop for more than 24 hours on a trip from Melbourne. The Airbus ultra-long range A350-1000 flight was followed by more than 3.6 million people on jet tracking site FlightRadar24 alone. The non-stop journey from Melbourne to Toulouse took 24 hours and 24 minutes. Airbus said the aircraft, which boasts a unique 20,000-litre extra fuel tank, remained in the air for 24 hours and 24 minutes, covering 23,075 km without stopping, before landing at the plane’s factory in Toulouse, France. A source with knowledge of the flight said it is the longest flight flown by an Airbus aircraft. However, the company is still evaluating the data with the relevant authorities to determine if this also qualifies as an official world record.



The Guinness Book of World Records currently lists a 2005 flight of a Boeing 777 from Hong Kong to London as the longest in the world. A Boeing 777-200LR Worldliner flew 21,601.7 kilometres non-stop and without refuelling from 9 to 10 November 2005 in 22 hours and 42 minutes in “the longest flight ever by an unmodified commercial aircraft”. View post on X Flight-tracking provider Flightradar24 said the trip was the second-most-tracked flight ever on its channels—behind a 2024 flight carrying Queen Elizabeth II’s coffin. “A total number of 3,652,947 people tracking it home, making it our second most tracked flight ever!” FlightRadar24 posted. The A350-1000 ULR is a specially modified model that is being built for Qantas to fulfil its “Project Sunrise” specifications, which will allow direct, non-stop flights between Sydney and London and Sydney and New York.



Qantas has ordered 12 of the aircraft. When active in Qantas’ fleet, the A350-1000 ULR will be able to travel directly between Sydney and London, either flying up over parts of the Eurasia, across Europe or over the Pacific and then the North Pole. The fastest Sydney-to-London flight would be 19 hours and 25 minutes, and the slowest is about 21 hours, Qantas officials have said. From London to Sydney, it would take between 18 and 20 hours. The time of the flight would vary “from day to day” and its “hugely influenced by winds,” Qantas’ chief technical pilot Alex Passerini told a gathering in Toulouse in June. Related Article Review Alan Joyce’s self-serving tell-all packs plenty of action, attitude and drama



The plane, still in its primary coating, was flown to Melbourne last by four Airbus flight test pilots, and five flight test engineers, who will put “the aircraft’s systems through their paces”. Qantas pilots were expected to joined the Airbus flight test crew for the return journey to France. The aircraft completed its first flight on June 2, 2026. In the weeks since, Airbus’ test teams have carried out extensive testing on the ground and in the air in Toulouse, including of the aircraft’s redesigned fuel system. More to come with Reuters The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Charges laid after police chase comes to an end on train tracks in Perth’s east
World.content:
A 25-year-old Stratton man will face court on Wednesday after allegedly leading police on a chase through Perth’s east on Tuesday afternoon.

A police chase came to an end on the train line in Perth’s east on Tuesday. 9News Perth

Police allege the man was the driver of a Holden Trailblazer that failed to stop when officers attempted to pull the car over on Ferguson Street about 2.50pm.

The chase didn’t last long before the car hit a railway embankment, ending up on the train line near Farrall Road in Swan View.

Police allege the man fled the scene but was arrested nearby.

The 25-year-old man has been charged with reckless driving to escape pursuit by police, driver of a vehicle failed to comply with a direction to stop (circumstance of aggravation), and no authority to drive (disqualified from holding or obtaining).

He will appear before Perth Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

World.title: Perth house relocator arrested in ongoing dispute over allegations he owes clients millions
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACourts Perth house relocator arrested in ongoing dispute over allegations he owes clients millions Rebecca Peppiatt July 29, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth man who runs a house relocation company has been arrested and charged with breaching a civil court order after he allegedly ignored multiple attempts by magistrates across WA to engage in multiple financial disputes. James Sinclair Thomson, 35, is the owner of Perth House Relocators, as well as JT Projects and JST Projects Australasia. James Sinclair Thomson. Consumer Protection WA His business relocates “pre-loved” homes, setting them up with development plans, council approvals, renovations, additions, site earthworks and plumbing installation. Other business names associated with Thomson include 1800 Houses, Perth Oversize Relocators, Buildtech Marine and Civil, Disaster Mitigation, and Perth Skip Bins.



But a growing lists of disgruntled customers claim Thomson has not honoured contracts, takes deposits without supplying them with a house, owes contractors pay for work, and hotels for accommodation and food. Now Consumer Protection has released a warning against engaging with Thomson after nine separate complaints were made to the watchdog who claim he took more than $1 million in payments and failed to deliver the contracted services. “We have received multiple detailed complaints alleging that Mr Thomson accepted very large sums of money but failed to deliver the homes or complete the work he promised, leaving consumers financially and emotionally distressed,” Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake said. “In several cases, homes were delivered but left unassembled or uninhabitable, while in others no home was delivered at all despite invoices being paid in full.” Last month, WAtoday exclusively revealed that Thomson was being sued by multiple clients, with default judgments issued after he failed to engage with the legal processes.



Thomson told this masthead at the time that he did not receive any of the paperwork because they had been sent to the wrong address. Related Article Exclusive

Construction Perth house relocator leaves trail of clients, contractors claiming he owes millions His legal issues were later compounded by allegations he assaulted one of the aggrieved complainants, who confronted him at a worksite in Bridgetown claiming Thomson owes him $120,000 for a house he never received. During that confrontation, Josh Aylett alleged that Thomson tailgated him for 40 kilometres to Nannup, T-boned his car and pepper-sprayed him in the face. Thomson was arrested and charged with dangerous driving, no authority to drive, possessing a controlled weapon, endangering the life, health and safety of a person, and cause poison to be administered. Thomson pleaded not guilty to the allegations, as well as failing to comply with a direction and contravening the provisions of a planning scheme.



On Sunday night, however, he was slapped with two more criminal charges after he was arrested at a Baskerville property east of Perth and charged with two counts of “an arrested person who, without reasonable excuse, contravened his or her undertaking commits an offence”. Those charges relate to the default civil judgments that have been made against him. Thomson spent Sunday night in the lock-up before appearing in Perth Magistrates Court on Monday. During that hearing, he told the magistrate a civil judge had told him he should not have been on bail and that “gentleman that’s suing me over a forklift sent my documents to the wrong address”. Thomson was told he needed to get legal advice but declared he did not and would instead plead not guilty and then “try and get the prosecutor to discontinue it on public interest”.



He was released on bail with a $100 personal undertaking and no bail conditions. James Sinclair Thomson. One of his alleged complainants, who asked not to be named, said Thomson has allegedly repeatedly used “delay tactics” to evade being brought to justice. She claims Thomson is “wasting considerable public resources in all his court cases”, and alleges that “overall he’s making a mockery of the system”. Others who have spoken to this masthead but asked to remain anonymous include tradesmen who worked for Thomson but claim they were never paid, including one electrician who claims Thomson owes him $14,000 for work across five jobs.



Meanwhile, the Jurien Bay Hotel has blacklisted Thomson and commenced legal action, claiming he owes more than $2500 in unpaid bills. When contacted by this masthead about the group’s claims last month, Thomson said his highly successful business had poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into communities up and down the state, and had thousands of happy clients in the four years it has been operating. Thomson said he had engaged his own lawyer to sue those who had allegedly made defamatory comments about him online, and said their complaints had turned into a witch hunt that had forced the closure of his social media and bank accounts after they were reported as dodgy. “There’s a couple of contractors that have been caught up in this who we do owe money to,” he said. “But we can’t pay them because the clients aren’t paying us. Our income stopped, or not stopped completely, but stopped to the point where I think we turned over [$5 million] or $4 million last year, and so that’s dramatically gone down in the last few months.



“So there’s a couple of contractors caught up who we do owe the money to, and we are litigating that, and have told them what’s happening.” Editor's pick WA courts Can you have a private conversation in a pub? The law is about to be tested Thomson claimed he would be getting the default judgments against him set aside because he was not properly served the paperwork. Blake urged the community to exercise caution and avoid engaging Thomson, or any of the businesses he trades under, for house relocation services. “Given the scale of the alleged losses – more than $1 million across nine consumers – and the recurring issues reported, it is important that Western Australians are alerted to the risks of dealing with this trader,” the commissioner said.



Those who believe they have been affected by Thomson’s conduct are urged to lodge a complaint on the Consumer Protection website.

World.title: Queensland parliament updates: Mining and regions on the estimates menu
World.content:
Before we get into today’s updates, a reminder of what we learned yesterday, after the evidence of Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren.

Reports from the ABC last month highlighted the lack of First Nations directors in the state’s two largest hospital and health services.

Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren at Tuesday’s estimates hearing. Queensland parliament

Yesterday, Rosengren claimed the lack of legally required First Nations members on three hospital service boards was the result of “unscheduled vacancies” after a major overhaul of all 16 HHS boards.

As we report though, those departures were all either forced or known in advance.

(They also come amid accusations the Crisafulli LNP has sought to unpick Indigenous representation and policies in a push dubbed “Project Invisibility”.)

World.title: 24-hour retail and no default noise limits in major push to revitalise Brisbane’s nightlife
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Default sound limits imposed on live music venues will be reviewed, as a landmark report into reinvigorating Brisbane’s nightlife recommends introducing 24-hour retail options, scrapping ID scanning at smaller venues and introducing facial recognition technology to speed up long lines for patrons.

Queensland’s inaugural Night-Life Economy Commissioner, former Powderfinger bassist John “JC” Collins, handed the state government his major Moonside report outlining efforts to ease the pressure on smaller music and entertainment venues back in February.

The state government says it will introduce reforms to make Brisbane’s nightlife more vibrant. Markus Ravik

The state government released the report on Wednesday, saying it would implement a Nightlife Economy Action Plan to revitalise Brisbane’s nightlife.

Among the recommendations, Collins has suggested noise compliance action only be taken after five separate household complaints, default noise limits be reviewed and noise standards be updated based on land-use zones rather than residential rules.

World.title: Operation Rosny ICAC investigation LIVE updates: Former Liberal Party staffer Dylan Whitelaw continues evidence after bombshell claim over Opposition Leader’s donation to NSW Reformers
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day three of the public Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry codenamed Operation Rosny. The inquiry is examining a broad range of allegations including branch-stacking, possible illegal donations and other behaviour involving Liberal figures, property developer Jean Nassif, Catholic Schools NSW and Sydney councils.

We are expecting to hear more from former Liberal Party operator Dylan Whitelaw, a former member of “The Reformers” faction who gave evidence yesterday.

Here’s a recap of what we heard on Tuesday:

Text messages from a Reformers group chat showed then-Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney wanted to “shake down” Angus Taylor for $10,000 in donations.

A text message shown at the inquiry showed Dylan Whitelaw telling the group chat that McInerney had received a commitment “from Angus” for a “15k injection, plus a 3k monthly donation”.

A spokesperson for Taylor did not deny the donations were made, but said “donations and fundraising activities are declared in accordance with the rules and are a matter for the party”.

Whitelaw told the commission he and employee Robert Assad did Liberal party factional work during their working hours at Catholic Schools NSW. It was a “running joke” between himself and Assaf, Whitelaw said.

Michael O’Hara, who the commission has heard provided financial support to the Reformers, withdrew his support after feeling then-premier Dominic Perrottet and prime minister Scott Morrison had gone too “woke”.

O’Hara said he now feels his support of the Reformers was a “mistake”, and he was “disgusted” after hearing allegations outlined in Monday’s hearing.

Stay with us for our live coverage, and you can watch the proceedings live-streamed here.

World.title: ‘No-one’s vaping in the gym’: Doueihi apologises for Tigers walkout as he and Marshall address club culture
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘No-one’s vaping in the gym’: Doueihi apologises for Tigers walkout as he and Marshall address club culture Dan Walsh and Adrian Proszenko Updated July 29, 2026 — 10:10am ,first published July 29, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adam Doueihi has apologised to Tigers fans and his teammates after controversially standing himself down from playing as coach Benji Marshall addressed allegations of players using e-cigarettes during training sessions. Doueihi returned to training on Tuesday and addressed teammates, having clashed with Marshall over the coach’s decision to move him from the halves for last week’s game against the Raiders, which the Tigers lost 56-10. Adam Doueihi returned to Wests Tigers training on Tuesday. Audrey Richardson An irate Doueihi took the opportunity to speak his mind, telling the coach he was fed up with the lack of accountability and professionalism that had led to another failed NRL campaign, and told Marshall he would not be playing against Canberra. Doueihi raised several issues over standards at the club, though refused to elaborate on Wednesday morning as he reiterated that he is committed to his three-year deal with the Tigers and is not eyeing an early exit.



“I should’ve played,” Doueihi said, conceding he took Marshall’s positional call “the wrong way”. “It hurt watching the boys on the weekend that I wasn’t out there … I’ve had a really, really good conversation with Benji, Shaun and the club about my care-factor for the club. Adam Doueihi and Benji Marshall at training on Tuesday. Audrey Richardson “I play and wear my heart on my sleeve. I know it’s hard for our fans to see. I let them down on the weekend. “I’m happy to wear all the criticism … Did I want to bring that noise to the club? No, that wasn’t my intention. I had a really good conversation with [my teammates] after.”



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Tigers name Adam Doueihi at halfback for Eels clash Minutes earlier, Marshall denied suggestions of double standards among the playing group, as well as reports that Tigers players have been vaping in the gym, claiming the stories were “fabricated”, but acknowledged players using e-cigarettes is an issue for the club. “There are issues that if they are issues, we’ll definitely address internally among the players,” Marshall said. I can tell you now that no one’s vaped in the gym, that’s actually fabricated or misinformation. “Is there a vaping problem? Probably with players, but like with young men, you can’t tell them whether to vape or smoke or whatnot, and I definitely can’t control what they do 24/7, and I’m not with them all the time, so I don’t feel like there’s a culture problem. “If we’re talking about standards and that, there’s probably a few things we might have walked past recently that we need to address ... whatever the concerns were from Adam’s perspective, they were all dealt with in the room.”



Marshall said his decision to recall Doueihi immediately into his starting side against the Eels, at the expense of rookie Javon Andrews, was the best call in pursuit of a win. “I didn’t feel disrespected [by Doueihi’s withdrawal],” Marshall said. “What I could see was a young guy who needed support and wasn’t in the head space to play … I saw a guy who was hurting and who wasn’t in the position to play. You can’t force that.” The development came just 24 hours after Doueihi held peace talks with Marshall, chief executive Shaun Mielekamp and football manager Pat Richards, with the rugby league news cycle dominated by the latest drama to engulf the joint-venture. More to come.

World.title: Victorian Labor leadership LIVE: Premier Ben Carroll mulls cabinet appointments following Jacinta Allan’s resignation
World.content:
As politicians arrive at Spring Street for another sitting of Victorian Parliament, Labor MPs congratulated Jacinta Allan on her long career in politics after The Age reported last night she would not recontest her seat of Bendigo East.

“I congratulated her on an incredible career and as a great servant of the Labor Party and as a woman who has made an extraordinary contribution to the people of Victoria,” said former health minister Mary-Anne Thomas, an ally of Allan.

Former health minister Mary-Anne Thomas last year. Simon Schluter

“It’s always moving when a dear friend and a person who has served with such distinction, their career comes to an end. But I’m sure that she’s looking forward to some much-needed time with her family.”

Ports Minister Melissa Horne, who had privately advocated for a royal commission, thanked Allan for her service but said the leadership change was “an opportunity to reset”.

World.title: Millions tune in as Qantas jet completes 24-hour non-stop flight
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Millions tune in as Qantas jet completes 24-hour non-stop flight Chris Zappone July 29, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas’ Project Sunrise plane has touched down in Toulouse after flying non-stop for more than 24 hours on a trip from Melbourne. The Airbus ultra-long range A350-1000 flight was followed by more than 3.6 million people on jet tracking site FlightRadar24 alone. The non-stop journey from Melbourne to Toulouse took 24 hours and 24 minutes. Airbus said the aircraft, which boasts a unique 20,000-litre extra fuel tank, remained in the air for 24 hours and 24 minutes, covering 23,075 km without stopping, before landing at the plane’s factory in Toulouse, France. A source with knowledge of the flight said it is the longest flight flown by an Airbus aircraft. However, the company is still evaluating the data with the relevant authorities to determine if this also qualifies as an official world record.



The Guinness Book of World Records currently lists a 2005 flight of a Boeing 777 from Hong Kong to London as the longest in the world. A Boeing 777-200LR Worldliner flew 21,601.7 kilometres non-stop and without refuelling from 9 to 10 November 2005 in 22 hours and 42 minutes in “the longest flight ever by an unmodified commercial aircraft”. View post on X Flight-tracking provider Flightradar24 said the trip was the second-most-tracked flight ever on its channels—behind a 2024 flight carrying Queen Elizabeth II’s coffin. “A total number of 3,652,947 people tracking it home, making it our second most tracked flight ever!” FlightRadar24 posted. The A350-1000 ULR is a specially modified model that is being built for Qantas to fulfil its “Project Sunrise” specifications, which will allow direct, non-stop flights between Sydney and London and Sydney and New York.



Qantas has ordered 12 of the aircraft. When active in Qantas’ fleet, the A350-1000 ULR will be able to travel directly between Sydney and London, either flying up over parts of the Eurasia, across Europe or over the Pacific and then the North Pole. The fastest Sydney-to-London flight would be 19 hours and 25 minutes, and the slowest is about 21 hours, Qantas officials have said. From London to Sydney, it would take between 18 and 20 hours. The time of the flight would vary “from day to day” and its “hugely influenced by winds,” Qantas’ chief technical pilot Alex Passerini told a gathering in Toulouse in June. Related Article Review Alan Joyce’s self-serving tell-all packs plenty of action, attitude and drama



The plane, still in its primary coating, was flown to Melbourne last by four Airbus flight test pilots, and five flight test engineers, who will put “the aircraft’s systems through their paces”. Qantas pilots were expected to joined the Airbus flight test crew for the return journey to France. The aircraft completed its first flight on June 2, 2026. In the weeks since, Airbus’ test teams have carried out extensive testing on the ground and in the air in Toulouse, including of the aircraft’s redesigned fuel system. More to come with Reuters The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Charges laid after police chase comes to an end on train tracks in Perth’s east
World.content:
A 25-year-old Stratton man will face court on Wednesday after allegedly leading police on a chase through Perth’s east on Tuesday afternoon.

A police chase came to an end on the train line in Perth’s east on Tuesday. 9News Perth

Police allege the man was the driver of a Holden Trailblazer that failed to stop when officers attempted to pull the car over on Ferguson Street about 2.50pm.

The chase didn’t last long before the car hit a railway embankment, ending up on the train line near Farrall Road in Swan View.

Police allege the man fled the scene but was arrested nearby.

The 25-year-old man has been charged with reckless driving to escape pursuit by police, driver of a vehicle failed to comply with a direction to stop (circumstance of aggravation), and no authority to drive (disqualified from holding or obtaining).

He will appear before Perth Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

World.title: Perth house relocator arrested in ongoing dispute over allegations he owes clients millions
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACourts Perth house relocator arrested in ongoing dispute over allegations he owes clients millions Rebecca Peppiatt July 29, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth man who runs a house relocation company has been arrested and charged with breaching a civil court order after he allegedly ignored multiple attempts by magistrates across WA to engage in multiple financial disputes. James Sinclair Thomson, 35, is the owner of Perth House Relocators, as well as JT Projects and JST Projects Australasia. James Sinclair Thomson. Consumer Protection WA His business relocates “pre-loved” homes, setting them up with development plans, council approvals, renovations, additions, site earthworks and plumbing installation. Other business names associated with Thomson include 1800 Houses, Perth Oversize Relocators, Buildtech Marine and Civil, Disaster Mitigation, and Perth Skip Bins.



But a growing lists of disgruntled customers claim Thomson has not honoured contracts, takes deposits without supplying them with a house, owes contractors pay for work, and hotels for accommodation and food. Now Consumer Protection has released a warning against engaging with Thomson after nine separate complaints were made to the watchdog who claim he took more than $1 million in payments and failed to deliver the contracted services. “We have received multiple detailed complaints alleging that Mr Thomson accepted very large sums of money but failed to deliver the homes or complete the work he promised, leaving consumers financially and emotionally distressed,” Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake said. “In several cases, homes were delivered but left unassembled or uninhabitable, while in others no home was delivered at all despite invoices being paid in full.” Last month, WAtoday exclusively revealed that Thomson was being sued by multiple clients, with default judgments issued after he failed to engage with the legal processes.



Thomson told this masthead at the time that he did not receive any of the paperwork because they had been sent to the wrong address. Related Article Exclusive

Construction Perth house relocator leaves trail of clients, contractors claiming he owes millions His legal issues were later compounded by allegations he assaulted one of the aggrieved complainants, who confronted him at a worksite in Bridgetown claiming Thomson owes him $120,000 for a house he never received. During that confrontation, Josh Aylett alleged that Thomson tailgated him for 40 kilometres to Nannup, T-boned his car and pepper-sprayed him in the face. Thomson was arrested and charged with dangerous driving, no authority to drive, possessing a controlled weapon, endangering the life, health and safety of a person, and cause poison to be administered. Thomson pleaded not guilty to the allegations, as well as failing to comply with a direction and contravening the provisions of a planning scheme.



On Sunday night, however, he was slapped with two more criminal charges after he was arrested at a Baskerville property east of Perth and charged with two counts of “an arrested person who, without reasonable excuse, contravened his or her undertaking commits an offence”. Those charges relate to the default civil judgments that have been made against him. Thomson spent Sunday night in the lock-up before appearing in Perth Magistrates Court on Monday. During that hearing, he told the magistrate a civil judge had told him he should not have been on bail and that “gentleman that’s suing me over a forklift sent my documents to the wrong address”. Thomson was told he needed to get legal advice but declared he did not and would instead plead not guilty and then “try and get the prosecutor to discontinue it on public interest”.



He was released on bail with a $100 personal undertaking and no bail conditions. James Sinclair Thomson. One of his alleged complainants, who asked not to be named, said Thomson has allegedly repeatedly used “delay tactics” to evade being brought to justice. She claims Thomson is “wasting considerable public resources in all his court cases”, and alleges that “overall he’s making a mockery of the system”. Others who have spoken to this masthead but asked to remain anonymous include tradesmen who worked for Thomson but claim they were never paid, including one electrician who claims Thomson owes him $14,000 for work across five jobs.



Meanwhile, the Jurien Bay Hotel has blacklisted Thomson and commenced legal action, claiming he owes more than $2500 in unpaid bills. When contacted by this masthead about the group’s claims last month, Thomson said his highly successful business had poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into communities up and down the state, and had thousands of happy clients in the four years it has been operating. Thomson said he had engaged his own lawyer to sue those who had allegedly made defamatory comments about him online, and said their complaints had turned into a witch hunt that had forced the closure of his social media and bank accounts after they were reported as dodgy. “There’s a couple of contractors that have been caught up in this who we do owe money to,” he said. “But we can’t pay them because the clients aren’t paying us. Our income stopped, or not stopped completely, but stopped to the point where I think we turned over [$5 million] or $4 million last year, and so that’s dramatically gone down in the last few months.



“So there’s a couple of contractors caught up who we do owe the money to, and we are litigating that, and have told them what’s happening.” Editor's pick WA courts Can you have a private conversation in a pub? The law is about to be tested Thomson claimed he would be getting the default judgments against him set aside because he was not properly served the paperwork. Blake urged the community to exercise caution and avoid engaging Thomson, or any of the businesses he trades under, for house relocation services. “Given the scale of the alleged losses – more than $1 million across nine consumers – and the recurring issues reported, it is important that Western Australians are alerted to the risks of dealing with this trader,” the commissioner said.



Those who believe they have been affected by Thomson’s conduct are urged to lodge a complaint on the Consumer Protection website.

World.title: Queensland parliament updates: Mining and regions on the estimates menu
World.content:
Before we get into today’s updates, a reminder of what we learned yesterday, after the evidence of Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren.

Reports from the ABC last month highlighted the lack of First Nations directors in the state’s two largest hospital and health services.

Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren at Tuesday’s estimates hearing. Queensland parliament

Yesterday, Rosengren claimed the lack of legally required First Nations members on three hospital service boards was the result of “unscheduled vacancies” after a major overhaul of all 16 HHS boards.

As we report though, those departures were all either forced or known in advance.

(They also come amid accusations the Crisafulli LNP has sought to unpick Indigenous representation and policies in a push dubbed “Project Invisibility”.)

World.title: 24-hour retail and no default noise limits in major push to revitalise Brisbane’s nightlife
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Default sound limits imposed on live music venues will be reviewed, as a landmark report into reinvigorating Brisbane’s nightlife recommends introducing 24-hour retail options, scrapping ID scanning at smaller venues and introducing facial recognition technology to speed up long lines for patrons.

Queensland’s inaugural Night-Life Economy Commissioner, former Powderfinger bassist John “JC” Collins, handed the state government his major Moonside report outlining efforts to ease the pressure on smaller music and entertainment venues back in February.

The state government says it will introduce reforms to make Brisbane’s nightlife more vibrant. Markus Ravik

The state government released the report on Wednesday, saying it would implement a Nightlife Economy Action Plan to revitalise Brisbane’s nightlife.

Among the recommendations, Collins has suggested noise compliance action only be taken after five separate household complaints, default noise limits be reviewed and noise standards be updated based on land-use zones rather than residential rules.
