World.title: Flashes of light, thunderous booms as possible fireball crosses North Island
World.content:
People have reported seeing bright flashes of light and hearing thunderous booms as a fireball crossed over the lower North Island.

Fireballs Aotearoa director Steve Wyn-Harris said the fireball, or large meteor, crossed the lower North Island at 10.26pm on Tuesday.

Wyn-Harris said many people who had heard it told them the fireball got low enough into the earth's atmosphere to potentially drop a meteorite or meteorites onto the ground.

Did you see the fireball? Send your pictures to iwitness@rnz.co.nz

He said members of their team were currently going through the data that their cameras collected last night.

"Once that is done, we will have a much clearer idea whether this meteoroid got low enough and slow enough to stop burning up, go into dark flight and also where it may have landed," he said.

A screenshot of video filmed from Toatoa, Ōpōtiki, in Bay of Plenty, showing a fireball on the far right of the image. Supplied / David Greig

"However, early analysis has the north facing cameras in the lower North Island looking into a nearly full moon and the south facing cameras are inundated with the size of the terminal flash making gathering useful data to identify where a meteorite may have fallen difficult."

People across the country posted on social media that they had seen or heard the fireball.

"It was huge, the ball was orange with a purple tail," one person from Tūrangi said.

"Saw a bright green ball falling down and turning orange at the end," said another in Auckland.

A person from Ruby Bay said it sounded like "someone hit a wheelie bin with a stone".

"Sounded like a cross between a train not running on the track with a bit of thunder mixed in," said a person in Carterton.

World.title: Human Rights Commission warns Treaty clause overhaul increases legal uncertainty
World.content:
The Human Rights Commission (HRC) is urging the government to scrap its planned amendment of Te Tiriti o Waitangi clauses, warning it could create more confusion and deepen division.

In a submission published on Tuesday, the Commission said the government's proposals were "constitutionally regressive" and risked weakening Treaty protections.

In May, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the coalition would change or remove references to the Treaty of Waitangi in 19 pieces of legislation "in the interests of increasing certainty and supporting compliance".

But HRC Indigenous Governance Partner Dayle Takitimu said it would have the opposite effect.

Human Rights Commission Indigenous Governance Partner Dayle Takitimu. Te Kāhui Tika Tangata Human Rights Commission

"The government said it wants clarity, but many Māori, legal experts, the Waitangi Tribunal, the Human Rights Commission, and international bodies say the review risks doing the opposite: weakening protections, reducing accountability, and increasing conflict.

"Achieving clarity - if that is the aim of the exercise - doesn't require watering down obligations to the bare minimum.

"Certainty and clarity are better achieved by following agreed human rights standards which support honouring treaties and respecting Indigenous peoples' human rights."

The Commission concluded that the government's plan downgraded Te Tiriti obligations and was "likely to increase, not reduce, uncertainty and litigation risk."

The changes risked intensifying racial tension and harming Crown-Māori relations, it said.

It also criticised the review, which recommended the changes, saying Māori had not been properly consulted throughout.

The review was secured by New Zealand First during coalition negotiations with National after the last election.

The Commission called on the government to abandon its changes and instead work with Māori on any replacement.

"Te Tiriti is not a side issue or a drafting inconvenience; it is part of the constitutional and human rights foundation of Aotearoa," Takitimu said.

RNZ has approached Goldsmith for comment.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In May, the government announced it would remove references to the Treaty principles in seven pieces of legislation.

Another 10 would be watered down, and two made "more specific".

At the time, Goldsmith said iwi would be consulted, and all New Zealanders could have their say through the select committee process.

"Over the last 30 or 40 years, Parliament has made all sorts of references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Sometimes it's 'honour', or 'have regard to', or 'give effect to', or 'take into account'," Goldsmith said.

World.title: Art brings tikanga Māori to one of Auckland's busiest streets
World.content:
New Māori art is bringing tangata whenua narratives into the heart of Tāmaki Makaurau, ready to welcome in thousands of visitors who will descend on one of Auckland's busiest streets.

People will now be able to see and touch two new taonga toi (public art) which were blessed and unveiled at a formal dawn ceremony led by Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei early on Wednesday morning.

When the City Rail Link (CRL) is open, thousands of train passengers will arrive at street level through the north-eastern exit from Te Waihorotiu Station, and immediately be welcomed by toi Māori.

Wāhine is a 3.7 metre bronze sculpture of a Māori woman performing a karanga (call of welcome), and is created by master carver Arekatera 'Katz' Maihi and weaver Beronia Scott.

Maihi (Ngāti Whātua) told RNZ the statue will allow Māori to see themselves in the centre of Auckland.

"It's important to have this type of mahi in the public spaces because we all hear the current debates around the country, and this is just a total reminder that you can say whatever you want, you can take away what you want, but you'll never move us. We're going nowhere, we're here forever."

Maihi said since Wāhine will likely be the first thing people see as they exit the new Te Waihorotiu Station he had to incorporate the welcoming process into its design.

"It was all about utilising our practices and our tikanga in these spaces."

Master carver Arekatera 'Katz' Maihi and weaver Beronia Scott. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Beronia Scott (Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei) said the inspiration for the korowai (cloak) that Wāhine wears came from a korowai they have at the marae.

"I've always been told by master weavers that a korowai is called korowai because of the hukahuka (tassels). A lot of people get that mixed up, they think everything's korowai, so that's why I didn't put anything else on it besides the hukahuka, so that they have to say the right word."

Maihi said the statue will be a "friend" for the statue that currently stands at Te Komititanga, the public square in front of Waitematā train station, creating an equal balance of tāne and wāhine.

"That also is the reason why I decided I wanted to really acknowledge our wāhine. They've been missing from this sort of space.

"I te tuatahi he tohu maumahara, he tohu whakanui ki ngā mahi o ngā wāhine katoa i roto i tō tātau nei hapori o Tāmaki nei. E hoki ake ngā whakaaro ki ngā kuia o mua tae noa ki ēnei rangi, ō mātau nā whaea e mahi ana i ngā mahi."

"The wāhine artists, Māori, it's hard to see, hard to find them. So my cousin [was] grabbing me, and I'm very reluctant to do all of this stuff. I'm all good weaving, I'm fine there, I'm all good in that space, but I think wāhine and Māori especially need to be acknowledged," Scott said.

"She stands on a low plinth, scaled and oriented to meet the gaze of manuhiri (visitors) as they ascend the ramp from the underground station."

Surrounded by his mokopuna, renowned Māori sculptor and carver Chris Bailey hopes the new mahi toi will serve as a meeting place and create lasting memories for future generations. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Further along Victoria Street West on the corner Queen Street stands Horotiu, a 7.2-metre-long tuna kūwharuwharu (longfin eel) cast in silicon bronze and depicted spiralling downward from Puna Kauariki, the celestial spring.

Renowned Māori sculptor and carver Chris Bailey (Ngāti Paoa, Te Aupōuri) said the towering bronze tuna was designed to reconnect people with the history beneath one of Auckland's busiest intersections.

"I want to say that it was a mana whenua collective that shoulder tapped me to be part of this," he told RNZ.

"They said, 'We don't care what you do, bro, as long as it's unmistakably Māori, if you don't understand English or Māori language.' I think they were thinking about everyone that comes down here."

He said the decision to create a tuna kūwharuwharu came after researching what Te Waihorotiu looked like before Tāmaki Makaurau was urbanised.

"The reason why I came up with a tuna kūwharuwharu, or longfin tuna, is the fact that Horotiu used to come down through here."

Bailey said every whakairo should reflect the history of the place where it stands.

"Whenever I do whakairo, we have to look at the whakapapa of the whenua, so that it relates to the area."

Rangahau (research) into the area's geological history showed a volcanic eruption had diverted the Waihorotiu stream thousands of years ago, creating wetlands that were once abundant with tuna.

"In order to come up with what we did come up with, a tūna, we looked at the geographical footprint of this place, pre-European, and that told us that a volcanic eruption occurred, pushing a big lava flow down here, which is why we use this water feature as a bit of lava, and dammed up Horotiu up by Aotea Square, and that became a big, like a swamp area, and it drained off down around the corner and come down here.

"And we realised that the tūna were just, there was just heaps and heaps of life here, back in the day, pre-European."

He said the waterway had never truly disappeared.

Horotiu, a 7.2-metre-long tuna kūwharuwharu (longfin eel) cast in silicon bronze stands along Victoria Street West on the corner Queen Street. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

"With my partner [Sally Smith] who I collabed with, she was an architect working on these two towers, and the engineers on these towers were continuously pushing the water out of the basements. And with that in mind, and the creative process, I thought, holy heck, that's Horotiu. It's still pushing its way.

"Even though this whole place is compressed with infrastructure, Horotiu is still trying to push its way into the present."

Surrounded by his mokopuna, Bailey hoped the mahi toi would serve as a meeting place and create lasting memories for future generations.

"I was looking through some of our photographs. Some of our photographs at home, and we've got photos of me at the zoo with my sisters sitting on the mouth of this big dragon.

"I thought to myself, man, we've got to make one of these, but we'll make it in our own flavour - an iconic piece or a wayfinder where people can come and take photos and say, 'I'll meet you at the eel.'"

He hoped tamariki growing up in Aotearoa would have memories of the sculpture similar to those he had of climbing on public artworks as a tamaiti.

"When I grew up, there weren't any Māori sculptures around the place.

"They were all celebrating Pākehā cricket guys or guys that had survived the Second or First World War, and all kudos to that. I understand that. This is our time now.

"This is our time now… keep more Māori putting their creative thumbprint into the whenua for us."

World.title: US demand for apple industry robotics driving change at Hawke's Bay manufacturer
World.content:
A surge in global demand for robotics and AI from the apple industry is driving big changes for a Hawke's Bay robot manufacturer.

Hawk Technology is making the robots in Hastings, then shipping the machines to the US where apple packhouses in Washington are lining up to get them.

General manager Sam Combs told RNZ it had built a few hundred machines for the New Zealand market over the past few years, and now the US market is really taking off.

Sam Combs. RNZ / Alexa Cook

He said the first 50 Gen 5 Apple Packers had been installed in Washington, with another 250 on order.

"The American market's about seven times the size of New Zealand for apples only. Washington's the Hawke's Bay equivalent of New Zealand and grows about two-thirds of the fruit.

"So we've gone and focused on that area. And yeah, the demand at this stage is greater than our manufacturing capability," said Combs.

It's a far cry from where it all began more than 30 years ago when Combs' grandad was collecting kerbside recycling to process and export for his business, All Brite Industries

The Comb family bought Hawk Packaging and began turning the recycling into the cardboard trays that sit between layers of fruit when it's boxed up in packhouses.

Avocado trays made from recyled paper and cardboard. RNZ / Alexa Cook

"We had customers start coming to us and say, 'hey, look, you supply your trays in bundles of 175 trays, and we've just got someone essentially standing there grabbing a tray and putting it onto a conveyor belt, is there some way that you can automate that for us'?"

The first machine they designed was a 'Tray Denester' which seperates out a bundle of apple trays, then they created a 'Tray Inserter'. But it's the third product that's been the most popular - the Robotic Apple Packer.

With 15 AI cameras working simultaneously, the robot inspects the fruit for any flaws and places it into cardboard trays according to its colour and quality.

"Probably where most of the IP sits is how we handle the fruit... it presents stem and calyx to the cameras so the guys upstairs can take photos and do the defects.

"This is quite a special piece of development, and is big part of what makes the machine so attractive," said Combs.

The Gen 5 Apple Packer in action. Supplied

The entire process is done on site in Hawke's Bay.

"We've got a full design team in-house. We've got fabrication in-house, and electricals in-house.

"A big philosophy of ours is just keeping everything here. We didn't want to have to send stuff overseas, and we wanted our design team and our fabrication team and our assembly team in the same room," he said.

And while the robots are replacing some packhouse workers, Combs said for many employers it's solved a labour shortage problem.

"In New Zealand it was a real problem for our customers to even find that labour in the first place, so it's there to complement their existing workforces," he said.

A Gen 5 Apple Packer being built. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Alan McDonald from the Employers and Manufacturers Association agreed, he said while there's been an increase in workplaces using AI and robots - it hadn't resulted in fewer jobs overall.

"I know there's a lot of concern about AI replacing people, but what we've seen in the past is that's not the case - there's displacement, re-training and different skills required, but more or less the same numbers are retained in the workplace.

"The common thing that we're hearing is that the issue with AI is it still needs human oversight and human input to work effectively in the workplace - so it's about how do we adjust those tasks, how do we re train our people," said McDonald.

It's the topic of a conference being held in Auckland on Tuesday night, called 'Workforce 2030', helping employers prepare for the increased use of AI.

"There's a reordering as people get used to working with these new tools and AI is just a tool... so how does that redesign the task or the job to accomodate both?," he said.

Ben Kloosterman is a senior machatronics engineer for Hawk Technology. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Seven years ago Hawk Technology had just two research design and development staff, which has grown to a team of over 50 workers to keep up with the growing demand for robotics.

Senior mechatronics engineer Ben Kloosterman has been with the company several years and is working on the Gen 5 Apple Packer.

"I'm currently writing machine codes, that's the software that runs on the machine and drives the packing behaviour of that machine, which involves everything from moving motors, vision processors from the cameras, inference to the AI models that we create and develop here," he said.

He's excited about where technology is headed.

"Previously with industrial automation it was always a bit frustrating cause the technology was like 20 years behind, so being free to learn and grow in that cutting edge technology is really really cool," said Kloosterman.

The next challenge Hawk Technology is keen to tackle, is robotics for the stone fruit industry.

World.title: David Tamihere faces two-month wait to find out if he will be retried
World.content:
David Tamihere will have to wait another two months to find out whether he will be retried over the 1989 murder of two Swedish backpackers in Coromandel.

Tamihere appeared at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday on the charges he was first convicted of in 1990 but which were quashed by the Supreme Court in March.

The Supreme Court said it was up to Crown prosecutors to decide whether to hold a trial again.

Crown prosecutor Alysha McClintock told the High Court on Wednedsay the Crown needed more time to decide whether it would try Tamihere again for the murder of Urban Höglin and Heidi Paakkonen.

Tamihere's lawyer James Carruthers said with a trial potentially a year away, the defence team was in the dark about the case.

They were dealing with events that happened 37 years ago and did not know what evidence or witnesses the prosecution was relying on.

Justice Mathew Downs agreed to the extension requested by the prosecution but gave it a deadline.

It must make a decision by the end of September, and Tamihere will appear again in October.

Arriving at court, Tamihere, who is now in his 70s, said he was feeling good but did not know what to expect.

He has been out of jail since 2010 when he was released on parole.

Crown solicitor Alysha McClintock at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

When the convictions were quashed, he was freed but is still facing the two murder charges.

Leaving court, Tamihere said he was not frustrated by having to wait longer - that it was "par for the course."

"I've gotten used to it - it's been 30-odd years or so," he said.

He was leading a normal life and "living quietly," he said.

The background

Höglin, 23, and Paakkonen, 21, were last seen in Thames in 1989.

Their disappearance and the subsequent trial was one of the country's highest profile crimes.

Many aspects remain a mystery.

Höglin's body was found in 1991, after Tamihere had been convicted, but Paakkonen's body has never been found.

At the time the couple went missing, Tamihere had been living in the bush in the Coromandel for about three years, in hiding from police over a prior rape charge.

Much of the Crown's original case was circumstantial.

It included evidence that Tamihere had been seen driving around the Coromandel region in the couple's ute.

Tamihere admitted dumping or selling their possession but maintained he had never met them.

The Crown's case also relied on testimony from former inmate Robert Conchie Harris who said Tamihere told him he killed the Swedes. However Harris was convicted of perjury over evidence in 2017.

The appeals

Tamihere first appealed his convictions in 1992, after Höglin's body was found wearing a watch that a prosecution witness had initially said he had seen at Tamihere's house.

The body was also 70km away from where the Crown first suspected he had been killed.

That appeal was unsuccessful but the 2017 perjury conviction of Harris prompted a new round of appeals from Tamihere.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal declined to quash the convictions, saying despite the problems with some crown evidence, there was still enough to safely say Tamihere was guilty.

The Supreme Court released its decision in March that finally quashed the convictions.

David Tamihere at the High Court session on Wednesday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

It said Harris's evidence meant the trial was fundamentally unfair, and that there had been a "radical recasting" of the crown case since the original trial.

That effectively meant the case had never truly been tested by a jury.

The court said it was possible a jury would still find Tamihere guilty, but that could only be decided in a retrial.

Timeline

April 1989 - Heidi Birgitta Paakkonen and Sven Urban Höglin are last seen in Thames. Tamihere was on the run from police and living rough in the bush after pleading guilty to raping a woman three years earlier.

May 1989 - David Tamihere is arrested over an earlier rape. That same day, the couple are reported missing.

December 1990 - Tamihere is convicted of murdering the couple and sentenced to life imprisonment.

1991 - Höglin's body is found near Whangamatā.

1992 - The Court of Appeal rejects Tamihere's appeal.

1994 - Tamihere is denied leave to appeal to the Privy Council.

1995 - Witness C - later revealed as Roberto Conchie Harris - swears an affidavit retracting his evidence.

1996 - Harris retracts his retraction.

2010 - Tamihere is released on parole.

2016 - A private prosecution alleges Harris lied at Tamihere's trial.

2017 - Harris is sentenced after being found guilty of perjury and not guilty of perverting the course of justice.

2017 - Harris appeals the perjury convictions and sentence and fights to keep his identity hidden.

2018 - Harris drops his appeal against the perjury convictions.

2018 - The High Court revokes suppression order for Witness B, another prison informant.

2020 - Justice Minister Andrew Little announces Tamihere's case is going back to the Court of Appeal after a Royal Prerogative of Mercy is granted.

November 2023 - The Court of Appeal hears Tamihere's case.

July 2024 - The Court of Appeal declines to quash Tamihere's convictions.

December 2024 - The Supreme Court grants leave for the case to be heard there.

August 2025 - The case heads to the Supreme Court sitting in Auckland.

World.title: 'Failures across services': How a 90-year-old was locked up 16 hours a day
World.content:
Warning: This story details elder abuse that some may find disturbing.

Health staff missed opportunities to help an elderly Christchurch man with advanced dementia who was being abused by his son, the health watchdog has found.

Norman Lee, 90, died weeks after police found him on a urine-stained mattress wearing adult nappies under a wetsuit in a dark, cold room in 2020.

His son, David Lee, had locked him in the room for up to 16 hours a day in conditions a judge likened to torture.

David Lee and another person were jailed in 2022 for abuse and neglect and for stealing more than $220,000 that was spent on cars, entertainment systems, scooters and holidays.

In findings released in May, coroner Mary-Anne Borrowdale stated the cause of Norman Lee's death was pneumonia and severe heart disease with a background of frailty and dementia and a context of elder neglect as a contributing factor.

In a case study published on Monday, the Health and Disability Commission (HDC) highlighted "systemic failures across services in recognising and responding to elder abuse risks, particularly where care occurs within a family setting".

Individuals are anonymised in the report but RNZ has confirmed the case relates to Norman Lee's care.

The commission said visiting health staff failed to escalate concerns about abuse.

The HDC pointed to Health New Zealand's poor record-keeping and case management continuity, lack of adequate staff support and supervision and gaps in processes for identifying and escalating elder abuse concerns.

"These failures contributed to missed opportunities to detect and respond to potential neglect," it said.

The HDC said HealthCare NZ provided regular weekly home domestic support, 15 minutes of daily support for meal preparation and twice-weekly personal care support for hygiene. Norman Lee also received support and oversight from Older Persons Mental Health at Health NZ.

"Three instances of concerns about possible neglect were raised in 2018 and 2019 and on each occasion initial inquiries found no evidence of abuse. The concerns raised were closed without further follow-up by any agency," the HDC said.

Workers failed to escalate concerns

During this period none of the individual workers involved in Norman Lee's care escalated concerns about abuse, and to the extent they queried practices in the home they received assurances from the family about care arrangements.

"In June 2020, after a hospital admission, a home visit by a Health New Zealand social worker revealed concerning living conditions, including restrictive and unusual measures (e.g. locked spaces, environmental controls outside the bedroom, camera monitoring, and use of a wetsuit at night). These issues were not previously escalated despite multiple service providers being involved," the report said.

The HDC found Health NZ and HealthCare NZ breached the code of health and disability services consumers' rights.

The commission said Health NZ failed to provide services with reasonable care and skill because of systemic issues.

The HDC recommended both organisations provide a formal apology and improve their processes.

"The commissioner acknowledged improvements implemented by Health NZ and HealthCare NZ in the six years that had passed since the events in response to the issues identified in this investigation," the report said.

Recommendations 'addressed and implemented'

A Health NZ spokesperson said the agency acknowledged the commission's findings.

"In line with our commitment to providing safe, high-quality care, all recommendations have been addressed and implemented," they said.

"Health New Zealand extends our deepest apologies to the family for their loss and recognise the profound impact of his death in 2020."

HeathCare NZ declined to comment.

World.title: First offshore oil exploration permit since ban lifted granted
World.content:
The government has granted Australian firm EnZed Energy a 12-year permit to look for oil in the Taranaki Basin.

It marks the first such permit granted since the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration was lifted almost a year ago, on 31 July.

Resources Minister Shane Jones announced the petroleum permit, which covers a 546 sq km area east of the Kupe gas field, in a statement on Wednesday, calling it a "major milestone".

"It is a clear signal that confidence is returning and investors are once again prepared to back New Zealand's resource potential," he said.

"Exploration does not guarantee a discovery, but it is an essential first step in understanding the resources New Zealand may have available to support future prosperity."

EnZed is expected to carry out a staged exploration, beginning with a study of seismic data and geological studies.

Jones' statement said the area included the Kaheru prospect, which was "a promising exploration target".

He said previous policy settings - presumably referring to the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration - had for too long discouraged investment in the sector, which "plays a critical role in supporting energy security, industrial activity and economic growth".

World.title: National, Labour unearth parental leave skeletons
World.content:
Political Panel: Nicola Willis and Vanushi Walters Morning Report Download MP3 12m

National is accusing Labour of appealing to "old-fashioned gender norms", while Labour says National has a "serious trust problem".

National over the weekend announced a policy to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30.

However, the party had voted against bringing in paid parental leave in 2001, voted against extending it from 12 to 14 weeks in 2004.

When in government in 2016 National extended paid parental leave from 14 to 18 weeks, but two months later then-Finance Minister Bill English controversially used a veto to block Labour's plan for a further extension to 26 weeks, and subsequently campaigned on an extension to 22 weeks.

English's successor as Finance Minister and National deputy leader Nicola Willis discussed the policy on Morning Report's weekly political panel alongside Labour MP Vanushi Walters.

Walters confirmed Labour would match the extension to 30 weeks, but still had to discuss wider policy changes - and the costings as part of its fiscal plan were "under discussion".

She pointed to National's previous track record on paid parental leave policies, saying the party must think women have a short memory.

"They've voted against it twice in the past ... just a year ago they introduced restrictions on pay equity that effectively mean that women can't be paid fairly, so to take so heavily on that side and give so little, I think women will remember that.

"They have a serious trust problem."

Walters acknowledge Labour had blocked Willis' former member's bill that would have allowed parents to share their leave entitlement, saying that was based on two studies from the UK.

"The advice at the time was that went against World Health Organisation advice in terms of women feeling comfortable that they could return to work and still continue breastfeeding ... there were two studies done in the UK, one before 2020 and one in 2023, which seemed to suggest that was true."

File photo. Labour Party MP Vanushi Walters says National has a "serious trust problem" on paid parental leave policies. VNP / Phil Smith

Walters said workplaces should be supporting women, but Labour still needed to discuss whether its position had changed on sharing leave.

Willis echoed the words of Prime Minister Christopher Luxon - who on Monday said "I don't know what happened in the past, I'm focused on the future" - noting neither she nor her leader had been MPs in 2016.

She said it was outrageous for Labour to oppose allowing parents to share their leave.

"It is 2026 and it is not just women who should be taking paid parental leave. And newsflash: not every woman can breastfeed or wants to breastfeed, and the idea that it is a government that gets to dictate to parents 'actually you need to stay at home and breastfeed', that is so old world."

"Parents should decide what is best for their child, and if that means mum says 'actually I've had a birth injury' and dad says 'I want to stay at home with you' ... it's outrageous that Labour would stand in the way of that and frankly appeals to some old-fashioned gender norms that I don't think have a place in a modern society."

Walters said that was not Labour's position.

Willis also pushed back on questions about why National had not extended parental leave or progressed her former member's bill - which has since been adopted by East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick - in this term of Parliament.

"Because we didn't get it into the coalition agreement," Willis said.

"What this underscores is, if people support these policies that we're putting forward, then really the best way to achieve them is to party vote National.

"We prioritised our economic and fiscal and tax plans; those were the core components ... in any coalition, you never get all of your policies across the line because you are having to compromise. There are two other parties at the table."

Opportunity

Willis also defended against questions about Luxon's decision to rule out any governing arrangements with the Opportunity Party - formerly known as TOP - which on multiple recent polls is just shy of having enough support to enter Parliament even without an electorate seat.

At the end of his weekly post-Cabinet briefing, Luxon indicated a "very, very strong position" about not wanting to work with the party - but pressed on whether this meant no kind of governing arrangement said it would not be a surprise National did not want to "do business" with them, before leaving the podium.

The ad-hoc nature of the announcement left Luxon to defend against questions about whether the decision had been made in the moment, without consulting his MPs.

Willis said the only people surprised by the move were the media.

"We've been saying for weeks that we oppose TOP's platform, which is based on a broad, swinging, massive new tax on every homeowner and landowner in the country," she said.

"Our position has been clear - in our caucus, across our membership - for a long time, and I think really the only people who were surprised by Chris Luxon being emphatic about that were the media, who want to keep the dream alive."

Pushed on whether it was a major decision to then rule the party out, Willis said National had "just made really clear that we don't want to do business with parties that want to increase taxes on working people".

Walters said Labour would set out which parties it could work with closer to the election, maintaining that "it's been unclear which way TOP will go".

Willis repeated that National would not work with Opportunity regardless of its openness to working with either.

World.title: 'The Aussies are on fire' on a night where that should've been impossible
World.content:
In the land of lochs, the announcer at Scotstoun Stadium couldn't figure out the first half of his name, but Lachlan Kennedy's performance on a sodden night in Glasgow ensured Australia will never forget it.

The weather on Tuesday night couldn't have been much more Scottish.

It was teeming basically all night, to the point the women's high jump final was halted for 45 minutes and the women's hammer throw probably should have been.

There were only two brief windows when the rain turned from a downpour to a drizzle, and it just so happened to be the moments "Lacklan" Kennedy was welcomed to the newly laid blue track.

The support crew was working overtime to make things vaguely manageable. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

It sounds like the sort of apocryphal tale told about Don Bradman in an era before the footage existed to prove your grandad was lying to you.

But it really happened.

To be clear, it wasn't dry, but no wetter than the night in March when he beat rising superstar Gout Gout in the 200m at the Maurie Plant Meet.

That established him once again as not just a fast runner, but a man capable of performing under the most intense pressure. A man plying his trade against a boy still figuring his out.

And Kennedy did it again on the biggest stage, winning Australia's first men's 100 metres medal at the Commonwealth Games with silver behind Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme on the second night of an athletics program that has been backed to deliver so much for Australia.

After not running a heat, Lachie Kennedy came straight out and made a statement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It's all about rising to the occasion. I'm a big believer in youp've got to bring your best when it matters most," Kennedy said.

"That's what we've been training for all season. We've all been planning for this competition here and my coach has clearly outdone himself."

It seems extreme to say he obliterated the national record of Patrick Johnson by taking it from 9.93 down to 9.85, but 0.08 of a second means something different to folks like Kennedy than it does us mere mortals.

In the 58 years since Jim Hines broke the 10-second barrier in the 100 metres, only 232 more have people dipped into single digits.

Aussie sprinters storm to 100m medals Lachlan Kennedy and Torrie Lewis set new national records in claiming 100m medals, while a host of Australians take gold across athletics and swimming.

The margins are so fine in the jewel in the athletics crown that there have been 1,550 legal runs in 0.42 of a second between 10 flat and Usain Bolt's world record of 9.58.

Most are from the United States, Jamaica and spread across Africa, and just two from Australia, with Kennedy the only one since 2003.

Kennedy stands alone in some respects, but is proud to be part of a pack pushing each other towards greatness.

Gout's rise trained a spotlight on the team, whose performances with that attention have proved it warranted.

"Aussie track is clearly in the best spot it's ever been, our team is so strong … We're in a real golden age," Kennedy said.

That was clearly evident as Kennedy — after running alongside compatriot Eddie Nketia, who finished sixth in the final after laying down a PB of 10.03 in the semis — was still talking to the media in the mixed zone when Torrie Lewis won bronze in the women's final.

Loading...

"The Aussies are on fire," Kennedy said as he cheered Lewis on to the team's third of six medals on the night.

Lewis also set a new national record, but rather than breaking a record that had stood for 23 years, hers had barely stood for 23 hours.

Lewis's 10.99 in the women's final came after her 11 flat in the semi, which lowered her own record of 11.04 from a week prior.

All in an event she wasn't even sure she wanted to compete in.

Torrie Lewis followed Lachie Kennedy into the history books. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Lewis is a beneficiary of the controversial automatic qualifiers into the semis of her pet 200m event, where she'll be hoping for more silver (or better) ware before the relays kick off in the ultimate representation of what this team can do.

"I have a day off tomorrow, luckily with the bye, then Thursday see how I pull up for the semifinal and hopefully I can do something special there as well," she said.

Lewis and Kennedy were the headlines due to Australia's historic lack of truly exceptional flat sprint talent since the days of Raelene Boyle.

We've jumped at a few false dawns and sometimes athletes have been unable to live up to those expectations, while field sensations like Steve Hooker, Nina Kennedy, Eleanor Patterson, Matt Denny, Nicola Olyslagers and a cavalcade of women's javelin chuckers have been consistently brilliant.

The anachronisms of the Commonwealth The Commonwealth Games continues to roll on despite calls to decolonise our lives, with Scotland of all places a strange venue to stage two celebrations of the British Empire over the past 12 years.

They were again on Tuesday night: Patterson and Olyslagers went 1-2 to continue their impossibly consistent excellence in the high jump, and 22-year-old Lara Roberts broke through for her first major international medal.

Patterson said it was "phenomenal" to see the runners joining the jumpers and throwers in contention for medals.

"I was out there and you get to have a lay of the land and you understand what's going on," she said.

"I definitely took in my stride that there was a lot of Aussies there and seeing how well everyone was doing.

"Athletics in Australia, it's going off. I want the whole of Australia to know that we're taking it to the world, we're representing Australia very well and we're not bad, we're pretty bloody good."

Back on the track Ky Robinson kicked off the stunning hour and a half with victory in the 10,000m

Australian athletics has had a number of these special nights of late, so much so that it risks becoming expected.

Australians have become so used to success in the pool that we have become somewhat blasé about the brilliance of our aquatic elite, but for now, on relatively dry land in Scotstoun there really is no other word for it.

That was special.

World.title: 'My time': Young gun Southam dethrones Chalmers in 100m final
World.content:
Kyle Chalmers has been dethroned as the Commonwealth Games 100m freestyle king in Glasgow, the "Big Tuna" having been reeled in by young friend and rival Flynn Southam in a landmark changing-of-the-guard moment.

With a potential record-breaking 10th Commonwealth gold in his sights, Chalmers had his proud record of never having been beaten by an Australian in major international competition dismantled by 21-year-old Southam in the Tollcross pool.

Southam's glory, fuelled by indignation at how he'd been somewhat dismissed as just a relay workhorse, set the tone for yet another medal-laden session of Dolphins' domination on the penultimate night of the program.

Jenna Forrester sealed her own golden treble in a remarkable breakthrough meet, adding a thrilling 200m individual medley triumph to the surprise 200m backstroke and 400m IM titles she'd already annexed.

And the night kicked off with 22-year-old Queenslander Kirralee Hayes taking the para gold medal in the 50m freestyle S13 final, and another Australian, Jenna Jones, taking bronze.

But Southam's win took pride of place, the young Fremantle-born, NSW-raised prospect finally fulfilling his potential as the most likely successor to "King Kyle", clocking a searing 47.13 seconds to bronze medallist Chalmers' 47.74. The pair were split by Welshman Matt Richards (47.64).

"Me and Kyle have utmost respect for one another. But it's my time to shine, and I know that," boomed Southam.

"I've been due for this, and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here as a little boy — but now I'm a man, and I belong here."

Flynn Southam says the Commonwealth Games are his breakout meet after winning gold in the men's 100m freestyle. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For Chalmers, though, cheered on by his wife, Norwegian international swimmer Ingeborg Loyning and baby daughter Astrid, there was a mixture of frustration that he couldn't land the 10th gold and 12th medal that would have taken him past the great Ian Thorpe as Australia's most successful men's swimmer ever at the Games.

Port Lincoln's 28-year-old maestro is likely to still have a chance, though, in the 50m butterfly final on the final day of competition in what could be his final appearance at the Games.

Admitting that he knew the passing-of-the-baton moment was inevitably coming at some point soon, Chalmers had hoped to delay it but was happy to tip his hat to the young gun after being the first to congratulate him.

"I'm completely fine with it," Chalmers said.

"I'd rather be in the race for that to happen than be retired and seeing them swim faster than maybe what… well, he hasn't quite got me just yet, but it's very close to what my best ever was.

"When we were able to sit in the medal presentation, I really said, 'You know, this is your moment. I'm so proud of you, enjoy your moment, enjoy singing the anthem.'

"I truly am so proud of him."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Southam had signalled his intentions at the start of the week when he clocked a sizzling lead-off relay leg of 47.09, which was just a hundredth of a second slower than Chalmers' all-time best and quicker than the South Australian star's 2026 best by half a second.

"It's pretty incredible. I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my success only comes from relays, and that's really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world," said Southam.

"Doubt always comes up, I was doubting myself as I was walking out, but it's about being able to turn that voice down and believing in yourself.

"I have Australia on my cap, I don't have just my name, so it's bigger than me."

Another medal came Australia's way with William Petric taking silver in the 400m individual medley behind New Zealand's double champion Lewis Clareburt.

AAP

World.title: 'Absolutely wild': Australian gymnasts top off Games with two more golds
World.content:
Breanna Scott and Jesse Moore have added to Australia's gold medal bonanza at the Commonwealth Games, taking out individual apparatus titles to finish their campaign in Glasgow.

Just minutes after Scott nailed a flashy balance beam routine to take out the title on her speciality apparatus, Moore hit every mark on the parallel bars to win another gold for Australia at Glasgow International Arena.

Scott scored 13.933 points for her routine, beating Singapore's Amanda Yap (13.233) and Lia-Monica Fontaine (13.00) of Canada.

Australian teammate and defending 2022 Birmingham champion Kate McDonald was last in eighth (12.166) after recovering from near-falls.

"[Balance beam] is definitely my favourite when it's going well," Scott said.

"It's kind of crazy, to be honest. It definitely hasn't sunk in yet.

"The last three days have just been absolutely wild.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

Scott wrapped up in Glasgow by winning her third medal and second gold medal.

She had contributed to Australia's dominant team all-around victory, before claiming silver in the women's individual all-around.

Backing up Scott, Moore found redemption on the parallel bars after missing the podium for the rings and pommel horse events.

Jesse Moore won his third gymnastics medal in Glasgow, winning gold in the men's parallel bars. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Australia's leading men's gymnast heading to Glasgow, Moore scored 14.000 points to pip Cypriot veteran Marios Georgiou (13.800 points) and Canada's Felix Dolci (13.300).

Scott and Moore's titles meant Australia medalled on every day of the five-day gymnastics competition in Glasgow.

Australia won nine medals, including four gold, behind Canada with 16 medals, seven of which were gold.

Moore said the gold medal was a weight off his shoulders.

"There's definitely been a bit of pressure building into these Commies with medal chances," Moore said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I knew I had one last crack to really have a go.

"This routine, I've done for years, so I could really trust myself and really go for it.

"I'm pretty stoked to get the gold."

The 23-year-old will leave the Games with three medals, having won a team bronze and an individual all-around bronze.

McDonald missed out on adding to her individual uneven bars gold and finished sixth in the floor routine final, ahead of 2022 Birmingham breakout star Georgia Godwin in seventh.

James Hardy settled for a fifth-placed finish on vault after claiming floor and rings bronze the day before, while 19-year-old Ritam Malik finished sixth on the parallel bars.

Australia's gymnastics medals

Gold (4): balance beam, uneven bars, team all-around (all women), parallel bars (men)

Silver (1): all-around (women)

Bronze (4): floor, rings, all-around, team all-around (all men)

AAP

World.title: 'Very bad look': Brisbane defender given three-game ban
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop has been suspended for three games for a serious misconduct act he admits is a "very bad look".

Gallop pleaded guilty at the AFL Tribunal on Tuesday night for what he described as retaliation on Mitch Georgiades after the Port Adelaide forward grabbed his broken thumb.

The 20-year-old had tackled Georgiades to the ground during Sunday's clash in Brisbane and, after the ball left the area, shoved the Port attacker face-first into the turf.

Gallop played the match with strapping on a broken right thumb.

"Mitch has grabbed my thumb as I have gone to stand up," Gallop said, adding Georgiades' action was intentional.

But Gallop expressed remorse for retaliating, saying he had phoned Georgiades to apologise.

"Looking back now and watching the footage, I understand that the retaliation to what happened wasn't fair," he said.

"I have gone out of my way to push him down, which I am sorry for and I do regret. I'd like to have that time over again.

"It's a very bad look and there's no room for it in footy."

Gallop said his retaliation was an "immediate reaction".

"I have grabbed the back of his jersey and pushed him back into the ground," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I think I play a hard brand of footy but I play a very fair brand of footy as well … it was purely out of retaliation."

Under questioning from the AFL's counsel Nick Pane, Gallop agreed his act was totally unreasonable and unacceptable.

Pane asked the tribunal for a three-game suspension.

"Georgiades' head made forceful contact with the ground," Pane said. "The action had significant potential to cause serious injury."

The Port spearhead wasn't hurt in the incident.

Gallop's counsel Adrian Anderson said the 23-gamer had "lashed out" but argued for a two-match ban.

"There is a context here," Anderson said.

"It's different where someone has a broken thumb and it's grabbed and they react in the heat of the moment."

After hearing just over one hour of evidence, tribunal chairman Jeff Gleeson KC and members Darren Gaspar and Scott Stevens returned a verdict some 50 minutes later.

AFL Saturday live North Melbourne survives a nervy finish to break a decade-long drought against Essendon as star ruckman Tristan Xerri rubs blood on Andrew McGrath's face in a heated exchange.

Gleeson said the tribunal gave no weight in its deliberations to Gallop's thumb being grabbed before his misconduct.

"The vision of the serious misconduct is startling in the degree to which it is unsportsmanlike," he said.

Gallop is the sixth AFL player suspended on a serious misconduct charge and the second this season, following North Melbourne ruckman Tristan Xerri's three-game ban for wiping blood onto the face of Essendon captain Andrew McGrath in a match in March.

Gallop will now miss Brisbane's games against Carlton, Hawthorn and Gold Coast, and will not be available until the round 24 games against Collingwood at the MCG.

AAP/ABC

World.title: National records tumble as Australia's athletics team stuns in Glasgow
World.content:
Eleanor Patterson won her second Commonwealth Games gold medal in the women's high jump on day five in Glasgow, leading home an Australian 1-2 on another stunning day for Australia.

Patterson was one of nine Australian gold medal performances, taking the team to 35 gold medals for the Games so far.

Twelve years after first triumphing in Glasgow as a teenager, Patterson equalled the Games record of 1.96m in a rain-interrupted final.

She managed the height with her third and last attempt before unsuccessfully attempting a new Games mark of 2m.

Patterson edged out Australian teammate and world champion, Nicola Olyslagers (1.93m).

Olyslagers failed with her three attempts at 1.96m and settled for silver.

On a big night at the main stadium, Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis both missed out on gold, but broke 100m national records while capturing medals.

Kennedy ended Australia's agonising wait for a men's Commonwealth Games 100m medal by taking silver.

GLASGOW, SCOTLAND - JULY 28: Lachlan Kennedy of Team Australia poses for a photo beside his new Area record in the Men's 100 Metres Final during the Athletics on day five of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium on July 28, 2026 in Glasgow, Scotland. (Photo by Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Australia's fastest man ran a personal best 9.85 seconds, beating Patrick Johnson's mark of 9.93 set in May 2003. It took a Games record to beat Kennedy, with Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme stopping the clock at 9.83.

Nigeria's Kayinsola Ajayi (9.90) was third, with Australian Eddie Nketia (10.06) back in sixth.

Lewis broke her own 100m national record in the semi-finals then broke it again in the final, finishing third in 10.99.

New Zealander Zoe Hobbs (10.93) won gold ahead of England's Amy Hunt (10.98).

Kennedy's silver was Australia's first medal in the men's 100m since 1962, when Michael Cleary took bronze.

Kennedy broke 10 seconds and lowered his personal best twice on the night, including a 9.94 in his semi, despite wet and windy conditions.

"It's all about rising to the occasion," Kennedy said after a wet and windy night.

"I'm a big believer in you've got to bring your best when it matters most. That's what we've been training for all season.

"To be able to come out here in those conditions, against a field like that, and to be able to run a time like that just goes to show how much faith I have in my team and all the people supporting me back home."

There was also joy for Ky Robinson, who completed an unprecedented 10,000m double for Australia when he finished strongly to hold off several rivals and claim gold.

Robinson won in 27:48.93 ahead of India's Gulveer Singh and Isle of Man's David Mullarkey.

GLASGOW, SCOTLAND - JULY 28: Gold medalist Ky Robinson of Team Australia celebrates after competing in the Men's 10,000 Metres Final during the Athletics on day five of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium on July 28, 2026 in Glasgow, Scotland. (Photo by Michael Steele/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

His triumph followed Rose Davies becoming the first Australian woman to win the event at the Commonwealth Games.

In the pool, Lani Pallister set a new Commonwealth Games record in winning her third gold of the meet.

Pallister won the 800m freestyle in a time of 8:11:12, beating New Zealand's Erika Fairweather.

Australia's Molly Walker took the bronze.

Pallister has now won the freestyle middle and distance triple — the 400, 800 and 1,500m freestyle.

In all, Australia won a total of five gold medals in the night session at Tollcross Swimming Centre.

In artistic gymnastics, Australia finished with two more gold, as Breanna Scott won the women's balance beam and Jesse Moore took out the men's parallel bars title.

Catch up on all the action from day five of the Games in our blog below.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Country footy player charged after 'ugly' scenes in southern WA
World.content:
A country football player has been charged with assault and choking after clashes during a game in southern Western Australia.

The man was allegedly involved in two incidents during Sunday's Lower South West Football League clash in Kojonup between the hometown Cougars and the Bridgetown Bulldogs.

Footage of two incidents during the game prompted public outcry and a police investigation.

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed Kojonup Police, with assistance from Busselton detectives, charged the man, from Cowaramup, with assault occasioning bodily harm and "impeding another person's breathing or blood circulation by applying pressure to the neck".

The Cowaramup man is accused of choking an opposing player. (Supplied)

On Tuesday WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch said violence on the football field was "not on".

"You are not immune on the sporting field," he said.

"We understand there are normal contacts in the spirit of play, but if it is outside of play and a deliberate targeted attack, then it is an assault."

Loading...

Game 'turned ugly'

Kojonup Football Club vice-president Matt Marinoni said the top-of-the-table clash was a "tense and fiery" game that "turned ugly".

He said the umpires did not see the off-ball incident.

"Then there was a lot of noise in the crowd," Mr Marinoni said.

"From there there was a bit of a wrestle and melee because we saw one of our teammates was on the ground, unconscious."

That player is in good spirits and recovering from his facial injuries and concussion, but is "shaken", according to the club.

A spokesperson from the Lower South West Football League told the ABC it was aware of the incident.

"The matter has been referred to the Country Football WA tribunal process and will be dealt with in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures," the spokesperson said.

The league declined to comment further, in order to "preserve the integrity and fairness of the tribunal process".

The Bridgetown Football Club said the matter was being dealt with by Country Football WA.

"[We] do not condone the behaviour shown during Sunday's game," the club said in a statement.

"This has no place in football and does not reflect the true values of our club."

The 23-year-old is due to face the Katanning Magistrates Court in August.

World.title: Joint spares Aussie blushes on tough day at Memphis Open
World.content:
Rising star Maya Joint has spared Australia's blushes at the WTA's hard-court event in Memphis.

On a day when the Australian challenge fizzled, the world number 77 won her round-of-16 clash against wildcard Whitney Osuigwe in straight sets.

The 20-year-old needed a tick over 90 minutes for a 6-4, 6-1 win against the American.

Joint will now meet the winner of top-seed Ekaterina Alexandrova or fellow Russian Kristina Liutova for a place in the quarterfinals.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Already boasting tournament victories in Rabat and Eastbourne last year, which helped her climb to a career-best number 28 in the world in February this year, Joint lost her serve twice in the opening set but did enough to take it in 45 minutes.

The second set proved more comfortable and Joint, who famously eliminated Serena Williams in the opening round of Wimbledon this year, broke three times to advance.

There was no such joy for Talia Gibson and Storm Hunter though.

Gibson was soundly beaten by German Tatjana Maria 6-0, 6-3, while compatriot Storm Hunter succumbed 7-5, 7-5 to fifth-seeded Colombian Camila Osorio.

World number 66 Kimberly Birrell, who lost her first-round doubles clash alongside American Peyton Stearns to Ingrid Martins and Ekaterina Ovcharenko 6-4, 6-7 (7/4), 11-9, takes on China's Ma Yexin in the singles draw on Tuesday.

In the shock of the day, Swiss third seed Viktorija Golubic was eliminated in three sets by Katie Volynets of the US, while all three unseeded Russian players in action were victorious.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Embattled LIV Golf tour asks to defer payment to Adelaide golf club
World.content:
The financially struggling LIV Golf tour has asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club, raising doubts over whether next year's Adelaide event will go ahead.

Kooyonga in Adelaide's western suburbs is scheduled to host LIV Golf Adelaide in 2027 before the tour moves to a newly redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course in 2028.

But the future of the league has been under a cloud since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced it would be pulling its reported billions in funding at the end of the 2026 season.

The Grange Golf Club has previously hosted the LIV event in Adelaide. (ABC News: Rory McClaren)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said he was made aware last week that LIV Golf had asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club.

"An extension was sought by LIV as they're working through programming next year for those payments to be made in September," he said.

"That extension was granted."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas says he is aware LIV Golf has asked for an extension. (ABC News)

Mr Malinauskas indicated there would "presumably" be enough time for Kooyonga to prepare for the March 2027 event, given the club had granted the payment extension.

The deferred payment is worth $500,000, Adelaide radio station FIVEaa reported.

In a statement, Kooyonga Golf Club confirmed it "evaluated and approved" a "short operational extension regarding its initial venue payment" to LIV Golf.

Deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague said the government needed to be more transparent about the event's future.

SA's deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague wants more transparency about the event's future. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

"Those who've bought tickets, those who are committing all sorts of other ways to the holding of the event are going to be left mightily disappointed … if all of a sudden LIV Golf goes from hero to zero," he said.

"If there's one thing you need to host successful international events, it's confidence and it's the capacity for everybody to get behind something because you know that it's actually going to happen and not just be shrouded in doubt.

"That's unfortunately where we stand right now."

The ABC has contacted LIV Golf for comment.

The shift to North Adelaide has been controversial. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The premier has previously said the state government would need a "clear indication" from LIV Golf about the event's future by October.

Can the SA government justify a $45m golf course upgrade without LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

The state government has a contract with LIV Golf until 2031 and pays an undisclosed fee for the tour to host an annual event in Adelaide.

LIV Golf's success at the Grange Golf Club was also the catalyst for the government to fund a controversial $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course.

The project has been subject to protests over the felling of 585 trees.

The government has since secured the Australian Open golf tournament to be hosted at the North Adelaide Golf Course from 2028 to 2034.

Tech.title: The US is banning foreign robots
Tech.content:
The US government is targeting China with a new import ban on “advanced robotic devices” and power inverters made in foreign countries, as reported earlier by Reuters. In an announcement on Tuesday, the Federal Communications Commission says the ban will include “mobile” robots, such as humanoid and quadruped models — but it is not limited to robots that walk around.

China is also home to the world’s leading power inverter producers — Sungrow and the already-blacklisted Huawei — which are often used in solar panel arrays and other renewable energy systems. In its announcement, the FCC cites “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” as the reason for the ban.

A FAQ page published by the FCC defines an “advanced robotic device” as a machine that is capable of “locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground;” comes with a sensor that perceives the surrounding environment; and has a chip for network connectivity. It must also weigh more than 4.4 pounds (including its docking station, if it has one).

By that definition, even future robot vacuums would automatically be banned if they do not obtain a waiver. The FCC does not appear to be limiting this ban to robots with legs. In fact, the National Security Determination that the FCC is using to justify the move explicitly mentions The Verge’s reporting on the poor security of DJI’s Romo robovac.

Similar to the US government’s ban on foreign-made routers, companies can request a waiver if they want to keep bringing new products into the US, but the waiver application does not include any requirements to improve the security of those robots or inverters. Existing products in the US also won’t be subject to the ban, so individuals and companies can keep on using existing robots and inverters.

Like previously, the US government seems to care primarily about where these devices are designed and manufactured before they get a waiver — and every applicant needs to provide a detailed plan to start manufacturing them in the United States instead. Sources tell Reuters that the FCC “is expected to exempt many non-Chinese suppliers from the restrictions.”

The FCC says today that all robots and power inverters can keep getting security and compatibility updates through January 1st, 2029 thanks to an additional waiver, but the agency is once again misleading the public about how those updates work. Companies do not currently need to inform the FCC when they push security updates to their devices.

Tech.title: Ariana Grande is suing the hackers who’ve been leaking her songs and videos for years
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ariana Grande filed a lawsuit on Monday in the Los Angeles County Superior Court against the currently unidentified hackers who allegedly stole and leaked private content. It aims to “uncover the identities of these currently unknown and unscrupulous individuals,” referred to as “John Doe 1 and John Does 2 through 100.” The lawsuit also says that “In 2023 alone, 45 unreleased songs” were “hacked, stolen, and leaked,” adding that hundreds of similar leaks have happened since Grande’s music debut in 2011.

The stolen content is said to include “still-in-production, unreleased masters and demos, footage from recording sessions, music videos, behind-the-scenes photographs and videos, as well as album and photoshoot outtakes.”

The lawsuit accuses the unidentified hackers of selling the content, as well as publishing it on social media platforms like X, TikTok, and YouTube. It claims their actions are invading her privacy and violating California’s Comprehensive Data Access and Fraud Act, a law against unauthorized computer access that has come up in cases including Sony’s lawsuit against George Hotz and Meta’s lawsuit against the Pegasus spyware.

As reported earlier by Variety, the lawsuit claims the hackers have repeatedly targeted people who work with Grande. In one incident in 2019, hackers stole Grande’s photos from a photographer’s Dropbox account. The following year, unreleased footage was stolen from a producer’s hacked “mobile device.” In 2024, scammers used phishing emails to get unreleased photos from a technician working with one of Grande’s photographers.

Tech.title: The union drive at the Wikimedia Foundation is expanding
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In June, UK staff at the nonprofit that runs Wikipedia became the first to announce their intention to form a union. Now, US-based employees at the Wikimedia Foundation are joining the union drive, but management at the nonprofit has declined to voluntarily recognize their union.

“While the Wikimedia Foundation touts to the public that they plan to take a neutral stance in our organizing efforts, they have already proven that not to be the case behind the scenes,” a press release sent by Communications Workers of America, with which Wiki Workers United is affiliated, reads in part. “When the Foundation rejected our request for voluntary recognition this week, they immediately sent out to employees and the public statements couched in classic union-busting rhetoric, rhetoric undoubtedly provided by outrageously expensive union-avoidance law firms. This insulting and wasteful use of Foundation resources is both an insult to Foundation employees and to the Free Knowledge Movement as a whole.”

In a public statement, the foundation said it believes a secret ballot election with the NLRB is the “appropriate path forward.”

The unionization efforts come at a time when tensions are high between the foundation and the thousands of unpaid volunteers who edit, write, and maintain Wikipedia. In May, hundreds of Wikipedia editors threatened to go on strike after the foundation dissolved an engineering team that worked closely with volunteers. Some volunteers questioned whether the layoffs were related to union efforts, which the foundation denied.

Tech.title: eBay’s bizarre cyberstalking saga ends with a $56 million settlement
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

eBay and three former executives will pay $55.7 million as part of a settlement with a Massachusetts couple targeted with a bizarre harassment and cyberstalking campaign in 2019, as reported earlier by CNBC. The settlement will resolve a lengthy legal saga that revealed how eBay’s former executives sent live insects, a bloody pig mask, a funeral wreath, and other strange items to David and Ina Steiner over their newsletter’s coverage of eBay.

The Steiners, who operate the EcommerceBytes newsletter, sued eBay and its former executives — including ex-CEO Devin Wenig — in 2021. The lawsuit accused the company and its executives of launching a coordinated effort to “intimidate, threaten to kill, torture, terrorize, stalk and silence” the Steiners in an attempt to “stifle” their eBay-related reporting.

The Department of Justice charged seven former eBay employees in connection with the harassment campaign in 2020, all of whom have been convicted. eBay agreed to pay a $3 million criminal penalty related to the case in 2024. Wenig wasn’t charged and says that he had no knowledge of the harassment.

“As we have long stated, what the Steiners were subjected to by former eBay employees in 2019 was wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened,” eBay says in a statement on its website. “We condemn, in the strongest terms possible, the employees who perpetrated and pled guilty to criminal charges for the misconduct against Ina and David Steiner.”

The $55.7 million settlement will include $46.15 million from eBay, $2 million from Wenig, $500,000 from former global operations SVP Wendy Jones, and $50,000 from former chief communications officer Steve Wymer. eBay will also donate $6 million to nonprofit organizations.

Tech.title: AI leaders sign a statement asking the government to do something about automated AI
Tech.content:
Employees of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as Google, Meta, Thinking Machines, Microsoft, Mistral, and other leading AI labs, have written a statement to the US government supporting a potential slowdown of sorts for frontier AI development — or at least a speed-up of global coordinated governance efforts.

“Al could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome is not guaranteed,” the employees wrote in the statement. “The world’s leading Al companies believe they could be close to automating Al research. It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate Al progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.”

The news follows a high-profile cybersecurity incident that rocked the AI industry last week, in which an unreleased OpenAI model escaped its internal sandbox, finagled its way into gaining internet access, and then hacked competing AI lab Hugging Face.

In the public statement, the employees went on to underscore the importance of some sort of coordinated regulation worldwide, so that the ever-intensifying AI race doesn’t outpace safety and monitoring tools.

“To realize Al’s potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight,” they wrote. “But each company—and country—is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress. Building on work already underway to monitor frontier model releases: We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated Al development.”

Some of the OpenAI executives or cofounders who have signed the statement include chief research officer Mark Chen, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, cofounder John Schulman, and cofounder Wojciech Zaremba. As for Anthropic, cofounder Jack Clark, cofounder Chris Olah, cofounder Ben Mann, and chief science officer Jared Kaplan have all signed, as well as Boris Cherny, who created and leads Claude Code, and Ethan Perez, who is Anthropic’s alignment team lead. OpenAI’s former chief futurist, Josh Achiam, and the former colead of its now-defunct superalignment team, Jan Leike, both also signed.

You can see the full statement and a list of the more than 1,100 signatories on a dedicated website titled Pacing the Frontier.

Tech.title: Is it illegal to trick the US government into wiping your phone during a questionably legal search?
Tech.content:
A Georgia man was charged with a felony for allegedly wiping his phone while being questioned by Customs and Border Protection. Samuel Tunick had something in common with others who have had their devices searched at airports: He was an activist.

Unlike others who have had their phones seized with no explanation, Tunick was told that CBP needed to search his device to determine whether it contained child sexual abuse material, according to court filings. But Tunick’s attorneys argue that the search “was a pretext for a fishing expedition” into his connections with the Stop Cop City protests in Atlanta, in which dozens of people were charged under state RICO laws, which were later dismissed. A few protesters are still facing domestic terrorism and arson cases.

According to a motion to suppress evidence filed in March, Tunick didn’t consent to a search and repeatedly asked to speak to his attorney, but CBP officers told him they didn’t need a warrant to search his phone. Tunick ultimately gave the agents the password to his phone, but when they entered it, “the screen went blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart,” court records say. Prosecutors allege that Tunick used the GrapheneOS “duress password” to wipe his phone, therefore deleting evidence.

Travelers’ devices have come under increased scrutiny since Donald Trump’s return to office — and the courts don’t agree on the legality of these warrantless searches. As a result, travelers have little clarity about how their rights apply at airports and other ports of entry. This gray area has allowed the Department of Homeland Security to target people perceived to be criticizing the president or the policies of his administration.

The confusion comes from a patchwork of federal rulings. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in United States v. Payne that law enforcement can forcibly unlock a person’s device with their fingerprint, facial recognition, or other biometric markers without running afoul of the Fifth Amendment’s protection against self-incrimination. But people can’t be forced to provide or enter their passcode, since it’s a form of “testimonial” evidence — information that requires a person to reveal their thoughts.

Those rulings, however, weren’t issued with airports in mind, and CBP claims that the Constitution doesn’t apply at ports of entry. Judicial opinion is mixed on that, too. The Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit — which oversees federal courts in Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia — recently ruled that border agents don’t need a warrant to manually search travelers’ phones. (More advanced forensic searches, however, do require a warrant.) A separate appeals court whose jurisdiction includes Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Puerto Rico ruled that agents can conduct manual and forensic searches without a warrant. Meanwhile, a federal judge in New York’s Eastern District determined that CBP agents can’t conduct any device searches without a warrant.

Tunick’s case has some details in common with the one that precipitated the New York ruling. The New York case began with a criminal investigation of Kurbonali Sultanov, a naturalized citizen from Uzbekistan whose name triggered an alert on the Treasury Enforcement Communications System, which identified him as a potential purchaser of child sexual abuse material. In court, Sultanov said agents told him he had no choice but to unlock his phone. He was also questioned by agents with ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations, who read Sultanov his Miranda rights, which he said he understood “50/50,” before questioning him.

It’s unclear why CBP agents believed Tunick had child sexual abuse material on his phone. The two-page indictment filed in a Georgia federal court makes no mention of it, and CBP did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

“Under the Fourth Amendment, a warrant should be required, or at a bare minimum, specific suspicion that there is illegal digital contraband on the device,” Nathan Freed Wessler, the deputy director of ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, told The Verge. “Agents should never be allowed to conduct warrantless searches on behalf of domestic law enforcement agents who just want to evade the normal Fourth Amendment requirement to get a warrant from a judge.”

The suspicion that immigration agents are surveilling activists has plenty of basis. In a lawsuit filed in Minnesota federal court, a Minneapolis labor organizer claimed that CBP was conducting “systematic” searches of activists’ devices, using counterterrorism as a pretext to keep tabs on the president’s left-wing critics. In March, more than a dozen members of a convoy that delivered humanitarian aid to Cuba had their phones seized at Miami International Airport.

Phone inspections at ports of entry are still relatively rare: CBP searched 55,318 phones and other electronic devices during the 2025 fiscal year, a 32 percent increase since 2023. (The US had more than 5 million international visitors in June 2025 alone, a figure that doesn’t include US residents.) But activists across the country have noted an uptick in surveillance since Trump returned to office, and the president has focused on cracking down on the left during his second term.

Last September, Trump issued an executive order designating “Antifa” as a domestic terrorist organization, even though there is no single organized entity known as antifa. In June a federal judge in Texas sentenced eight activists to upwards of 30 years in prison for supposedly belonging to an “Antifa cell.” The State Department recently issued a 100-page report alleging that several left-wing groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America, CODEPINK, and others were “front groups and fellow travelers” of the Cuban government. The report claimed that Cuba had influenced social movements in the US, including the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, and tied the Standing Rock and Cop City protests to “Antifa.”

As Trump’s crackdown on the left continues, activists who travel internationally may find themselves under additional scrutiny at airports and other ports of entry. Though US citizens can’t be barred from entering the country, CBP can seize their devices and attempt to break into them with advanced forensic tools. To prevent federal agents from accessing the contents of your phone, privacy experts suggest backing up and wiping your device — before traveling, not during an interrogation.

William Budington, a senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, explained that “a judge is not likely to view the use of a duress password sympathetically.” The EFF cautions against erasing the contents of your device mid-questioning, as Tunick is alleged to have done. “Factory resetting your device in your personal time is well within your rights.”

Tech.title: AI’s finally expensive enough to make Wall Street nervous
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.
